lessons.title: V3·NC1 — Worker threads and CPU-bound work
lessons.summary: One long synchronous function stops every request in the process. Worker threads give you a second V8 isolate to put that work in and a channel to talk to it. This sector covers the surface: structured clone, transfer lists, SharedArrayBuffer and Atomics, pooling, and cancelling work that refuses to yield.

# V3·NC1 — Worker threads and CPU-bound work

`02_event_loop` taught you the shape of the runtime: one thread runs your
JavaScript, and every callback waits behind the one currently executing. That
model is why Node is good at I/O — ten thousand sockets cost ten thousand file
descriptors and almost no threads — and it is exactly why one badly placed
`for` loop can take a service down.

Picture the failure precisely, because it is not the one people expect. A
report endpoint hashes a 20 MB payload, or renders a PDF, or runs `JSON.parse`
on a 60 MB body. The loop is busy for 400 ms. Nothing else in the process runs
during those 400 ms: not the other 300 in-flight requests, not the
health-check handler, not the heartbeat your orchestrator is waiting for.
Latency does not degrade smoothly — p50 stays fine and p99 falls off a cliff,
and eventually the liveness probe times out and something restarts a process
that was working perfectly well.

The fix is not "make the function faster". The fix is to run it somewhere that
is not the loop.

## Concept — a worker is an isolate, not a thread you share memory with

```ts
import { Worker } from "node:worker_threads";

const worker = new Worker(
  `const { parentPort, workerData } = require("node:worker_threads");
   parentPort.postMessage(workerData.a + workerData.b);`,
  { eval: true, workerData: { a: 1, b: 2 } },
);

worker.on("message", (sum) => console.log(sum));   // 3
```

That is a real OS thread, but the interesting part is what it is *not*. Each
worker gets its own V8 isolate: its own heap, its own module registry, its own
`globalThis`. Nothing is shared by default — not variables, not module state,
not your database pool. `worker_threads` is not pthreads with JavaScript
syntax; it is closer to a subprocess that happens to be cheap.

Cheap, not free. A worker costs roughly 5-15 ms and a few megabytes of heap to
start, because a fresh isolate has to be created and your entry module loaded
and compiled inside it. Spawn one per request and you have built a slower
version of the problem you were fixing. That is why the second half of this
sector is about pools.

**Four events, and you need all of them.** `message` for each `postMessage`,
`error` for an uncaught throw inside the worker, `messageerror` when something
arrives that cannot be deserialised, and `exit` with a code — `1` after an
uncaught error, `0` for a clean end, and whatever you passed to
`worker.terminate()` otherwise. A promise wrapper that listens only for
`message` hangs forever the first time the worker throws before it answers.

## Concept — how values cross the boundary

Three mechanisms, in increasing order of how much they ask of you.

**Structured clone (the default).** `postMessage(value)` serialises with the
structured clone algorithm: objects, arrays, `Map`, `Set`, `Date`, `RegExp`,
`BigInt`, typed arrays and cycles all survive. Functions, host objects,
sockets and class *identity* do not. Send an instance of your `Order` class
and the other side gets a plain object with the same fields — `instanceof
Order` is `false`, and any method you were relying on is gone. The cost is
proportional to the size of the graph, twice: once to write, once to read.

**Transfer.** Pass an `ArrayBuffer` in the transfer list and the memory is
handed over rather than copied:

```ts
const buffer = new ArrayBuffer(1 << 20);
worker.postMessage({ buffer }, [buffer]);
console.log(buffer.byteLength);   // 0 - this side no longer owns it
```

Zero-copy, constant time, and the sender's buffer is *detached*: it reports
zero length and any view onto it is dead. That is the whole point and the
whole trap. `Buffer` instances are views onto a shared pooled `ArrayBuffer`,
so transferring `buf.buffer` can detach memory belonging to unrelated buffers.
Allocate with `new ArrayBuffer(n)` or `Buffer.allocUnsafeSlow(n)` when you
intend to transfer.

**Share.** `SharedArrayBuffer` is genuinely shared memory: both threads read
and write the same bytes, with no message at all. Coordination becomes your
problem, and `Atomics` is the tool — `Atomics.add` for a race-free counter,
`Atomics.wait`/`Atomics.notify` for a blocking handoff. `Atomics.wait` throws
on the main thread, deliberately, because blocking the loop is the thing you
came here to avoid; use `Atomics.waitAsync`, which returns
`{ async: true, value: Promise }` or `{ async: false, value: "not-equal" }`
when the condition already holds.

## Concept — choosing between the three primitives

`worker_threads` when the work is CPU-bound JavaScript and you want shared
memory or comparatively cheap startup. `child_process` (next sector) when you
need a different program, a different runtime, or hard isolation — a crash in
a child cannot corrupt your heap. `cluster` (sector 3) when the unit of work
is *requests* rather than computation and you want N copies of the whole
server.

And the honest fourth answer: sometimes you should not parallelise at all.
`crypto` hashing, `zlib` and `fs` already run on the libuv threadpool, so the
async forms of those are off your loop before you do anything. Reach for a
worker when the expensive thing is your own JavaScript.

## Exercise 1 — one worker, one answer, no leaks

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `runOnce(source, workerData)` starts an eval worker,
resolves with its first message, rejects if it errors, and rejects if it exits
without saying anything. Every listener comes off on every path.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc01_worker_threads ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — dividing the work before you spawn anything

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `planPartitions(length, workers)` returns balanced
`[start, end)` ranges, spreads the remainder across the earliest partitions,
and never emits an empty range.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc01_worker_threads ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — a parallel map that keeps its order

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `sumInWorkers(values, workers)` partitions the input,
runs one worker per partition, and adds up the partials in input order rather
than completion order.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc01_worker_threads ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — transfer, and proving it happened

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `scaleInWorker(bytes, factor)` transfers a buffer into
a worker, has it scale every byte in place, transfers it back, and reports
whether the original was detached.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc01_worker_threads ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — shared memory and Atomics

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `countInParallel(workers, perWorker)` gives every
worker the same `SharedArrayBuffer`, has each one `Atomics.add` its share, and
waits for the total without blocking the main thread.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc01_worker_threads ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — a pool, because spawning is not free

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `WorkerPool` keeps at most `size` workers alive,
queues tasks beyond that, reuses idle workers, and reports `spawned`, `queued`
and `busy`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc01_worker_threads ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — cancelling work that will not yield

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `runCancellable(iterations, signal)` cooperates with
an `AbortSignal` through a shared flag, and falls back to `terminate()` when
the worker ignores it.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc01_worker_threads ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — progress on a channel of its own

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `runWithProgress(steps, onProgress)` hands the worker
one end of a `MessageChannel` for progress updates and keeps the result on the
main port.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc01_worker_threads ex8
```

## Challenge — a pool that can be told to stop

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. `createJobRunner({ size })` combines pooling,
the transfer list and cooperative cancellation into one API with per-job
signals and clean shutdown.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc01_worker_threads challenge
```

## Review — how did this worker actually end?

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. `settleWorker(worker)` reports the *first* thing
that happened — message, error, messageerror or exit — as a tagged object,
with every listener removed afterwards.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc01_worker_threads review1
```

# Reading - node/v3nc01_worker_threads

Threads in Node are not the threads you know from Java or C. Everything
surprising about them follows from one fact: a worker is a separate V8
isolate, and isolates do not share objects.

## Notes

**Startup is the number that decides your design.** Measure it once on your
own machine — `performance.now()` either side of `new Worker(...)` plus the
first `message` — and you will get something in the 5-15 ms range for a
trivial worker, more once your entry module imports half of npm. Against a
50 ms job that is 20-30% overhead; against a 2 ms job it is absurd. The rule
that falls out: pool for small jobs, spawn per job only when the job is long
and rare, and never spawn inside a request handler you have not measured.

**`workerData` is cloned at construction.** It goes through the same
structured clone as `postMessage`, which means a huge `workerData` makes
`new Worker()` slower, and mutations on either side after construction are
invisible to the other. `SharedArrayBuffer` is the exception — passing one in
`workerData` shares it, which is the standard way to hand a worker its
cancellation flag before it starts.

**`error` and `exit` are not alternatives.** An uncaught throw emits `error`
and then `exit` with code 1. A clean finish emits `exit` with code 0 and no
`error`. `terminate()` resolves with the exit code and stops the thread at the
next opportunity V8 gives it. A wrapper that settles on the first of the four
events, then unsubscribes, is the only shape that cannot hang.

**`terminate()` cannot interrupt a tight loop.** V8 stops a worker at an
interrupt point; a `while (true) {}` with no allocation and no call into the
runtime may never reach one. This is the single most misunderstood thing about
worker threads: you can *ask* a worker to die, and a sufficiently rude worker
will ignore you. Real cancellation is cooperative — a `SharedArrayBuffer` flag
the worker reads every N iterations — with `terminate()` as the escalation.

**Unref if the worker must not hold the process open.** `worker.unref()` takes
the thread out of the event loop's reference count, which matters for a
background worker in a CLI that should exit when the main work is done. Rerun
`ref()` before you await anything on it.

**`receiveMessageOnPort` drains synchronously.** It pulls one pending message
off a `MessagePort` without yielding to the loop, returning `{ message }` or
`undefined`. It is how you build a synchronous bridge over an asynchronous
channel — the trick `Atomics.wait` plus `receiveMessageOnPort` gives you, and
the reason some libraries can offer a blocking API on top of a worker.

## ex1 — the lifecycle wrapper

Four events, one settlement, and cleanup on all four paths. The version people
write first listens for `message` and `error`; it hangs when the worker exits
silently — a syntax error in the source, a `process.exit()` inside, an OOM.
Adding `exit` turns an invisible hang into a clear rejection, which is the
whole value of the exercise.

## ex2 — the partition arithmetic

Pure, tested, and worth doing before you touch threads because everyone gets
it slightly wrong. Integer division leaves a remainder, and dropping it means
losing elements; giving the remainder entirely to the last worker means one
thread does `k` extra items while the rest idle. Spreading it one item at a
time over the first `remainder` partitions is the balanced answer, and
clamping `workers` to `length` is what stops you spawning threads with nothing
to do.

## ex3 — order out of concurrency

`Promise.all` preserves *positional* order regardless of completion order, and
that is the entire trick: build the array of promises in partition order, then
`await Promise.all`. The failure mode this rules out — pushing into a shared
array from each `message` handler — produces a result that is correct in
testing, where the small partitions finish first, and wrong under load.

## ex4 — detachment as evidence

Checking `byteLength === 0` after the post is how you prove you transferred
rather than copied. It is also how you discover you did not: a transfer list
containing a `Uint8Array` instead of its `.buffer` throws
`DataCloneError`-shaped errors, and forgetting the list entirely silently
copies, which shows up only as a performance regression at 100 MB.

## ex5 — the counter you cannot race

`sharedView[i] += 1` from two threads loses updates: read, add and write are
three operations and the interleaving is real. `Atomics.add(view, i, 1)` is
one. The other half of the exercise is waiting without blocking:
`Atomics.waitAsync` gives you a promise, and it can return `not-equal`
immediately when the workers finished before you looked, which the naive
implementation forgets and then waits forever on a value that already arrived.

## ex6 — the pool

Three states — idle, busy, queued — and one invariant: the number of live
workers never exceeds `size`. The bug worth building the exercise around is
releasing the worker in a `finally`, so a task that throws does not lose a
worker from the pool permanently. Two failed tasks with a `size` of two and no
`finally` gives you a pool that accepts work and never runs it again.

## ex7 — cooperative cancellation

The shared `Int32Array` flag is the mechanism; the design point is that the
worker decides how often to look. Check every iteration and you pay an atomic
load per item; check every 10,000 and your cancellation latency is 10,000
iterations. Both are defensible; a worker that never checks is not.

## ex8 — a second channel

`MessageChannel` gives you `port1`/`port2`, and a port can be transferred into
a worker. The reason to bother rather than tagging messages on the main port
is separation: progress traffic never interleaves with results, the progress
consumer can be handed the port and know nothing about workers, and closing
the progress port ends the updates without touching the job.

## challenge — the three ideas together

A pool whose jobs each own a cancellation flag and a transferred payload. The
interesting decision is what an abort means for a job that is still queued:
it should never start, and it should reject immediately rather than waiting
for a worker to free up.

## review1 — classification instead of construction

Same lifecycle knowledge, opposite direction: rather than building a promise
that hides the events, you report which event won. It forces you to say out
loud what `exit` after `error` means, and why the first event is the only one
that matters.

## Further reading

- [`worker_threads` — Node.js API docs](https://nodejs.org/api/worker_threads.html) — the whole surface, including `receiveMessageOnPort` and `resourceLimits`.
- [`Atomics` — MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Atomics) — `add`, `wait`, `waitAsync`, `notify` and the memory model.
- [The structured clone algorithm — MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Web_Workers_API/Structured_clone_algorithm) — exactly what survives a `postMessage`.
- [`Transferable objects` — MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Web_Workers_API/Transferable_objects) — detachment, and what is transferable.
- [Don't block the event loop — Node.js guide](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/asynchronous-work/dont-block-the-event-loop) — the problem this sector solves, from the platform's own perspective.

# V3·NC1 — Worker threads and CPU-bound work (archive)

## Why a second thread exists at all

Node shipped without user-visible threads for nine years, and the official
answer to CPU-bound work was "use a child process". `worker_threads` arrived
behind `--experimental-worker` in Node 10.5 (2018) and became stable in Node
12. The motivation was not that processes could not do the job — they could —
but that they could not share memory, and passing a 200 MB image between
processes costs a full copy through a pipe both ways.

The design that landed borrows from the browser: an isolate per worker,
`postMessage` for communication, structured clone for values,
`SharedArrayBuffer` for memory. If you know web workers you already know
90% of this API; the Node-specific 10% is `workerData`, `resourceLimits`,
`receiveMessageOnPort` and the fact that a worker can require Node builtins.

## Worked example — the wrong fix and the right one

An endpoint that scores documents:

```ts
app.post("/score", (req, res) => {
  const score = scoreDocument(req.body.text);   // 300 ms of pure JS
  res.json({ score });
});
```

The first fix people try:

```ts
setImmediate(() => {
  const score = scoreDocument(req.body.text);   // still 300 ms, on the loop
  res.json({ score });
});
```

That moves *when* the loop is blocked, not whether. `setImmediate`,
`process.nextTick`, `await`, and wrapping in a promise all share this
property: the work still runs on the one thread. The only way to yield during
the work is to chop it into pieces and `await` between them, which changes the
algorithm and still costs the loop everything the pieces cost.

The real fix:

```ts
import { Worker } from "node:worker_threads";

const pool = new WorkerPool({ size: 4, script: new URL("./score-worker.js", import.meta.url) });

app.post("/score", async (req, res, next) => {
  try {
    res.json({ score: await pool.run({ text: req.body.text }) });
  } catch (error) {
    next(error);
  }
});
```

Four threads on a four-core box, a queue in front, and a loop that stays free
to accept connections. Note what did *not* change: the endpoint is still one
`await`, and the error path still goes through your normal middleware.

## Worked example — transfer versus clone, measured

```ts
const big = new ArrayBuffer(64 * 1024 * 1024);

const t0 = performance.now();
worker.postMessage({ big });                 // clone: allocates 64 MB, copies
const cloned = performance.now() - t0;

const t1 = performance.now();
worker.postMessage({ big }, [big]);          // transfer: pointer handoff
const transferred = performance.now() - t1;
```

On a typical laptop the first is tens of milliseconds and the second is
microseconds, and the second leaves `big.byteLength === 0` behind. Both
numbers matter: the clone is a real cost you can eliminate, and the detached
buffer is a real hazard you have to design around. A helper that transfers a
caller's buffer without documenting that it steals it will produce a bug
report titled "my array is empty after I call your function".

## Worked example — a cancellation flag

```ts
const flag = new Int32Array(new SharedArrayBuffer(4));

const worker = new Worker(source, { eval: true, workerData: { flag } });
signal.addEventListener("abort", () => Atomics.store(flag, 0, 1), { once: true });
```

and inside the worker:

```js
for (let i = 0; i < iterations; i++) {
  if ((i & 0x3ff) === 0 && Atomics.load(flag, 0) === 1) {
    parentPort.postMessage({ cancelled: true, done: i });
    return;
  }
  // ... work
}
```

`i & 0x3ff` checks every 1024 iterations, which costs approximately nothing
and bounds cancellation latency at 1024 items. This pattern is the answer to
the interview question "how do you cancel a running worker", and the honest
follow-up is that `terminate()` is the escalation when the worker is code you
do not control.

## Worked example — bounding a worker's blast radius

```ts
const worker = new Worker(entry, {
  resourceLimits: { maxOldGenerationSizeMb: 128, maxYoungGenerationSizeMb: 16 },
  argv: ["--strict"],
  env: { ...process.env, NODE_OPTIONS: "" },
});

worker.on("error", (error) => {
  if ((error as NodeJS.ErrnoException).code === "ERR_WORKER_OUT_OF_MEMORY") {
    metrics.increment("worker.oom");
    return respawn();
  }
  throw error;
});
```

Three separate protections in six lines. `resourceLimits` caps the worker's
heap, so a runaway transform kills its own thread with
`ERR_WORKER_OUT_OF_MEMORY` instead of taking the process's 4 GB with it. The
explicit `env` stops the worker inheriting `NODE_OPTIONS` you did not intend
it to have — inherited flags are a classic source of "it only misbehaves in
production". And handling `error` by *classifying* rather than rethrowing
turns a crash into a metric plus a respawn, which is the difference between an
incident and a graph.

The limit is per worker, not per process, and V8 enforces it with its own heap
limit machinery — so the failure arrives as a clean error event rather than an
OOM kill from the kernel, which you cannot catch at all.

## Common mistakes

- **Spawning a worker per request.** Startup dominates, memory climbs, and
  under load you fork-bomb yourself. Pool.
- **Listening for `message` only.** Silent exits become hangs.
- **Assuming class instances survive.** They arrive as plain objects. Send
  DTOs and revive on the other side, or send the fields you actually need.
- **Transferring a pooled `Buffer`'s `ArrayBuffer`.** You may detach memory
  another `Buffer` is using. Allocate for transfer with `new ArrayBuffer` or
  `Buffer.allocUnsafeSlow`.
- **Sharing a `SharedArrayBuffer` and using `+=`.** Lost updates. Use
  `Atomics`.
- **Calling `Atomics.wait` on the main thread.** It throws — by design.
- **Forgetting `finally` in a pool's release path.** A throwing task leaks a
  worker out of the pool.
- **Expecting `terminate()` to interrupt anything.** It stops the thread at an
  interrupt point, not mid-loop.
- **Leaving workers alive at shutdown.** The process will not exit; either
  `terminate()` them in your shutdown path or `unref()` them.

## Interview answer

*"When would you use worker threads?"*

When profiling shows a synchronous JavaScript function on the request path
that costs more than a few milliseconds — parsing, hashing, image work,
templating, compression you cannot delegate to `zlib`'s async API. Not for
I/O: that is already off-thread. I would pool the workers, because startup is
5-15 ms and a fresh isolate is megabytes; I would keep the payload small or
transfer an `ArrayBuffer` rather than clone it; and I would give every job a
`SharedArrayBuffer` cancellation flag, because `terminate()` cannot interrupt
a tight loop. If the work is really a separate program, or I need crash
isolation, I would use a child process instead — and if the bottleneck is
throughput of requests rather than one expensive function, the answer is more
processes, not more threads.

## Check yourself

1. Why does `setImmediate` not fix a CPU-bound handler?
2. What is the observable difference between a cloned and a transferred
   `ArrayBuffer` on the sending side?
3. Which four events can end a worker's life, and in what order do `error` and
   `exit` arrive?
4. Why does `Atomics.wait` throw on the main thread but not in a worker?
5. What does `Atomics.waitAsync` return when the value already differs from
   the expected one?
6. Your worker returns an object with a `toJSON` method and the receiver says
   it is not a function. Why?
7. How would you cancel a worker running a 30-second loop, and what are the
   two failure modes of the naive answer?
8. What is `receiveMessageOnPort` for, and why can it not be replaced by
   `port.on("message")`?
9. When does `worker.unref()` change the behaviour of your program?
10. How do you bound a worker's memory, and what error do you get when it goes
    over?
11. Why is `workerData` a poor place for a 100 MB payload?
12. Give a rule for choosing between `worker_threads`, `child_process` and
    `cluster` in one sentence each.

# The isolate boundary

The thing to understand about worker threads is that the boundary is not
between threads. It is between *isolates*, and V8 draws that line for reasons
that have nothing to do with Node.

A V8 isolate owns a heap, a set of compiled scripts, a garbage collector and
exactly one thread of execution at a time. Objects belong to their isolate;
there is no way to hand a pointer to a JavaScript object across the line,
because the receiving isolate's GC does not know about it, could not trace it,
and could not move it during compaction. This is not a missing feature. It is
what makes single-threaded V8 fast: no locks on property access, no barriers
on writes, a GC that can stop the world because the world is one thread.

So when Node's worker threads arrived, the boundary was already decided. What
Node added was the plumbing: a libuv thread per isolate, a `MessagePort`
implementation on top of a lock-protected queue, and the serialiser V8 already
had for `postMessage`.

## What crossing actually costs

`postMessage` runs V8's value serialiser, which walks the object graph and
writes a compact binary format — the same one behind `v8.serialize()`. It
handles cycles with back-references, preserves `Map`/`Set`/`Date`/typed-array
semantics, and refuses functions and native handles. On the other side the
deserialiser rebuilds the graph in the receiving heap. Two traversals, two
allocations of everything.

For a 1 KB object that is nothing. For a 50 MB nested structure it is a
noticeable pause *on both threads*, and it is easy to build a "parallel"
system whose serialisation costs more than the work. The measured rule of
thumb: if the payload is large and the computation is small, threads will lose
to doing it inline.

Transfer sidesteps the copy for `ArrayBuffer`, `MessagePort`, and a few other
transferables. Under the hood the backing store's ownership moves; the sending
`ArrayBuffer` is marked detached, its `byteLength` becomes 0, and every
`TypedArray` view onto it becomes a view onto nothing. `SharedArrayBuffer` is
different again: its backing store is reference-counted and genuinely shared,
so both isolates map the same pages. That is why `Atomics` exists at all — it
is the only defined way to order reads and writes between two threads under
JavaScript's memory model, which is a relaxed model borrowed from C++11.

`SharedArrayBuffer` has history worth knowing. It was disabled in browsers in
2018 after Spectre, and returned only behind cross-origin isolation headers.
In Node there was never a same-origin story to lose, so it has always been
available — one of the few places where the server platform is *less*
restricted than the browser.

## Threads, libuv, and what was already parallel

Node was never single-threaded in the strict sense. libuv keeps a threadpool
(four threads by default, `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` up to 1024) that runs
`fs` operations, DNS lookups via `getaddrinfo`, `zlib`, and the expensive
`crypto` functions such as `pbkdf2` and `randomBytes`. Network I/O does not
use it at all — epoll, kqueue and IOCP handle sockets on the loop thread.

This matters for deciding what to move. `await fs.readFile()` is already on
another thread. `crypto.scrypt` with a callback is already on another thread.
`zlib.gzip` async is already on another thread. What is *not* is your own
JavaScript, `JSON.parse`/`stringify`, `crypto.createHash(...).update(...)` on
a big buffer done synchronously, template rendering, and every regular
expression that backtracks. Those are the candidates.

A related trap: because the libuv pool is shared and small, a burst of
`fs.readFile` can starve `crypto.pbkdf2`, and a worker thread doing file I/O
competes for the same four threads as the main thread. Raising
`UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` is occasionally the whole fix for a service that looks
CPU-bound and is not.

## Pooling, and the numbers behind it

A pool exists because isolate creation is expensive in a way that is easy to
underestimate. You pay for: an OS thread, a new isolate and heap, the snapshot
deserialisation that gives you the built-ins, compiling and running your entry
module, and every `import` it pulls in. A worker whose entry file imports a
web framework can take 100 ms to become useful.

Sizing is the other half. The default that survives contact with production is
`availableParallelism()` minus one — leaving a core for the loop thread — with
a queue in front and a bound on the queue, because an unbounded queue converts
a CPU shortage into a memory leak. `os.availableParallelism()` (Node 18.14+)
respects cgroup CPU limits in a way `os.cpus().length` does not, which matters
enormously in containers: a pod limited to 1 CPU on a 64-core node will
happily spawn 63 workers if you ask `os.cpus()`.

`resourceLimits` bounds a worker's heap (`maxOldGenerationSizeMb`,
`maxYoungGenerationSizeMb`, `codeRangeSizeMb`, `stackSizeMb`). Exceeding it
kills that worker with `ERR_WORKER_OUT_OF_MEMORY` instead of taking the
process with it — the cheapest crash isolation `worker_threads` can give you,
and a good reason to run untrusted-ish transformation work in a worker even
when you do not need the parallelism.

## Termination, and the promise Node cannot make

`worker.terminate()` returns a promise and stops the thread — eventually. V8
terminates execution at interrupt checks, which sit at function entries, loop
back-edges that allocate, and calls into the runtime. Optimised code with no
allocation in the loop body can run for a long time between checks, and hand
written `while (true);` can run forever. There is no `pthread_cancel` here and
there should not be: killing a thread mid-mutation would leave the shared
memory you handed it in an unknown state.

So cancellation is a protocol, not a call. Shared flag, checked at a cadence
you choose; `terminate()` when the deadline passes; and a supervisor that
replaces the terminated worker, because a pool that loses a slot per timeout
degrades to nothing in an afternoon.

## The synchronous bridge

There is one more trick the API enables, and it explains why
`receiveMessageOnPort` exists at all. A worker can block: `Atomics.wait` is
legal off the main thread. So you can build a *synchronous* API on top of an
asynchronous service — the caller (in a worker) posts a request, calls
`Atomics.wait` on a shared slot, and the other side does the async work and
`Atomics.notify`s. The caller then drains the reply with
`receiveMessageOnPort`, which does not need a turn of the event loop to
deliver it.

This is how tools give you a blocking `readFileSync`-shaped API over something
that is fundamentally async, and it is worth knowing for one defensive reason:
if you see `Atomics.wait` in a stack trace on the main thread you are looking
at a `TypeError`, and if you see one in a worker you are looking at a thread
that is deliberately parked and will not respond to `postMessage` until it
wakes.

## When not to use worker threads

- **I/O-bound work.** More threads will not make the network faster. If your
  profile is mostly `epoll_wait`, add concurrency, not threads.
- **Small, frequent jobs.** Under about a millisecond of work, message passing
  and scheduling cost more than the job. Batch first, then thread.
- **Large payloads with cheap computation.** Serialisation eats the win.
  Transfer, share, or leave it inline.
- **When you need isolation from a crash or a native addon.** A segfault in a
  worker takes the process down; a child process is the boundary you want.
- **When the real problem is throughput.** Ten thousand requests per second on
  a four-core box is a `cluster` or replica-count question. Threads help one
  request; processes help all of them.
- **When a library is not thread-safe.** Native addons in particular: an addon
  that keeps per-process global state and was never audited for worker use
  will fail in ways that look like memory corruption, because they are.

The summary a senior engineer carries: workers are for *your* expensive
JavaScript, they cost milliseconds to create and copies to talk to, and the
only reliable way to stop one is to ask it politely and then be willing to
kill it.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 1 — one worker, one answer, no leaks

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function runOnce<T>(source: string, workerData?: unknown): Promise<T>
```

`source` is JavaScript to run with `{ eval: true }`. The promise settles on
the **first** thing that happens:

- a `message` → resolve with it;
- an `error` → reject with it;
- a `messageerror` → reject with an `Error` whose message mentions
  `messageerror`;
- an `exit` with no message first → reject with an `Error` whose message
  contains the exit code, e.g. `worker exited with code 1 before sending a
  message`.

On every path, remove every listener you added and make sure the worker is not
left running (`terminate()` after a rejection is fine and cheap).

```ts
await runOnce<number>(
  'require("node:worker_threads").parentPort.postMessage(6 * 7)',
);                                   // 42

await runOnce('process.exit(3)');    // rejects: "... code 3 ..."
```

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc01_worker_threads ex1
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the bug rather than the feature. Write the two-listener version
(`message` and `error`) and then ask what happens for each of these workers:

- `"process.exit(0)"` — exits cleanly, says nothing;
- `"throw new Error('boom')"` — errors, then exits with 1;
- `"syntax ~~ error"` — fails to compile.

The first one hangs forever. In production that is a request that never
answers and never logs, which is strictly worse than an error.

## Hint 2

`exit` always fires — after `error`, after a clean end, after `terminate()`.
So the `exit` handler is not an alternative to the others, it is the backstop
underneath them. That is exactly why you need the settle-once guard: `error`
then `exit` is one failure, not two.

## Hint 3

Leaked listeners on a dead worker do not matter; leaked *workers* do. A
`runOnce` that resolves and walks away leaves a thread alive if the worker's
code did not return, and the process will not exit while it lives. Decide
deliberately, and remember `terminate()` returns a promise you are allowed to
ignore.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 2 — dividing the work before you spawn anything

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export interface Partition { readonly start: number; readonly end: number; }
export function planPartitions(length: number, workers: number): Partition[]
```

Ranges are half-open (`start` inclusive, `end` exclusive), contiguous, and
cover `[0, length)` exactly. Sizes differ by at most one, with the larger
partitions first. Never return an empty partition: if `workers > length` you
return `length` partitions.

```ts
planPartitions(10, 3);  // [{0,4},{4,7},{7,10}]
planPartitions(9, 3);   // [{0,3},{3,6},{6,9}]
planPartitions(2, 5);   // [{0,1},{1,2}]
planPartitions(0, 4);   // []
```

`length < 0` or `workers < 1` throws a `RangeError`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc01_worker_threads ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two numbers do all the work: `Math.floor(length / workers)` is the base size,
and `length % workers` is how many partitions get one extra item. Everything
else is bookkeeping.

Notice that "spread the remainder" and "give it to the last one" produce the
same total and very different wall-clock times.

## Hint 2

Walk a cursor rather than computing each `start` from scratch:

```ts
let cursor = 0;
for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
  const size = base + (i < remainder ? 1 : 0);
  // ... use cursor and cursor + size, then advance
}
```

This makes contiguity true by construction, which is much easier to defend
than an index formula you have to re-derive every time you read it.

## Hint 3

Clamp before you divide: `const count = Math.min(workers, length)`. With that
line, `planPartitions(2, 5)` needs no special case, and `length === 0` falls
out as an empty array because the loop never runs.

The decision left to you: whether `Partition` is a class, an object literal or
a tuple. The gate reads `.start` and `.end`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the test. Whatever you write, these three properties must hold
for every input, and they are worth asserting in your own scratch file:

1. `sum(end - start) === length`;
2. `partitions[i].end === partitions[i + 1].start`;
3. `max(size) - min(size) <= 1`.

Property 3 is the one a naive implementation fails.

## Hint 2

The failure it fails with is worth picturing. Ten million items, four workers,
remainder handed to the last: three workers finish and idle while the fourth
grinds through its extra chunk. Your parallel speedup is capped by the slowest
partition, so imbalance is pure loss — this is the same reasoning behind
work-stealing schedulers, in miniature.

## Hint 3

`length === 0` is the input that separates a careful implementation from a
lucky one. Zero items, four workers: not four empty partitions, not one empty
partition, but no partitions at all — because spawning a thread to process
nothing is the purest form of overhead.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The ordering requirement is not a sorting problem. If you build an array of
promises in partition order and hand it to `Promise.all`, the result array is
in *positional* order by definition — completion order never enters into it.

The version that fails pushes into a shared array from inside each `message`
handler.

## Hint 2

Each worker needs its slice. Two ways to give it one: send the numbers in
`workerData`, or send the whole array plus a range and let the worker slice.
The second sounds cheaper and is not — `workerData` is structured-cloned per
worker, so sending the whole array to four workers copies it four times.

```ts
new Worker(source, { eval: true, workerData: { chunk: values.slice(s, e) } });
```

## Hint 3

The worker body is three lines: pull `workerData`, reduce, `postMessage`. Your
`runOnce` from ex1 is exactly the wrapper you want around it — reuse its shape
rather than rewriting the four-event dance per worker.

The decision left to you: what "no worker left running" means when one of five
rejects. `Promise.all` rejects on the first failure while the others are still
alive.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start by asking what makes this test non-deterministic if you get it wrong.
Four workers summing four slices will usually finish in roughly the order they
started, so an implementation that appends on completion passes locally and
fails on a loaded CI box. Concurrency bugs that only appear under load are the
expensive kind, and this is the smallest possible example of one.

## Hint 2

`Promise.all` has a property worth stating out loud: it preserves index, and
it rejects fast but does not cancel. The other four workers keep running after
the first rejection, and if nobody terminates them the process stays alive
holding four threads.

## Hint 3

Keep the `Worker` objects in an array as you create them, and in a `finally`
(or in the rejection path) call `terminate()` on all of them. Terminating a
worker that has already exited is harmless — it resolves with the exit code —
so you do not need to track which ones are still alive.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The transfer list is the second argument to `postMessage`, and it contains
`ArrayBuffer`s — not typed arrays. `worker.postMessage({ buffer }, [buffer])`
where `buffer` is `bytes.buffer`.

`workerData` cannot transfer, so this exercise needs a real `postMessage`
rather than the constructor shortcut.

## Hint 2

Inside the worker you get the buffer, wrap it, mutate it, and send it back
with its own transfer list:

```js
const view = new Uint8Array(message.buffer);
for (let i = 0; i < view.length; i++) view[i] = Math.min(255, view[i] * factor);
parentPort.postMessage({ buffer: view.buffer }, [view.buffer]);
```

Mutating in place is the point: allocating a second array in the worker throws
away half of what the transfer bought you.

## Hint 3

Detachment is observable without any special API — a detached `ArrayBuffer`
reports `byteLength === 0`. Capture the original length before you post, and
compare after.

The decision left to you: `bytes.buffer` may be larger than `bytes` when the
view has a `byteOffset` (which is normal for anything that came from Node's
`Buffer` pool). Decide what your function promises about that, and write it
down in a comment.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach it as a memory-ownership question rather than a messaging one. After
a transfer, exactly one thread may touch those bytes. The API you are writing
therefore *steals* its argument, and a caller who does not know that will file
a bug that reads "your function emptied my array".

That is a real design decision, and the reason libraries that transfer say so
in the first line of their docs.

## Hint 2

The trap in Node specifically: `Buffer.alloc(4).buffer` is usually an 8 KB
pooled `ArrayBuffer` shared with other `Buffer`s, and `byteOffset` is not
zero. Transfer it and you detach memory belonging to buffers you never heard
of, which produces corruption far away from this call.

`Buffer.allocUnsafeSlow(n)` and `new Uint8Array(new ArrayBuffer(n))` both give
you a buffer you exclusively own.

## Hint 3

Guard for it rather than hoping. If `bytes.byteOffset !== 0` or
`bytes.byteLength !== bytes.buffer.byteLength`, you are looking at a view into
someone else's buffer: copy it into a fresh `ArrayBuffer` first and transfer
that. Then `sourceDetached` honestly reports `false`, because you did not
detach the caller's memory — and the gate checks that you tell the truth.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 5 — shared memory and Atomics

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function countInParallel(workers: number, perWorker: number): Promise<number>
```

Allocate one `SharedArrayBuffer` holding a single `Int32Array` slot, hand the
same view to every worker via `workerData`, and have each worker perform
`perWorker` atomic increments. Resolve with the final value once every worker
has finished — which must be exactly `workers * perWorker`, every time.

Requirements:

- the counter is incremented with `Atomics.add`, not `view[0] += 1`;
- the main thread must not call `Atomics.wait` (it throws there); wait for the
  workers by whatever means you prefer;
- every worker is terminated or exited before you resolve.

```ts
await countInParallel(4, 50_000);   // 200000, deterministically
```

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc01_worker_threads ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`view[0] += 1` compiles to a load, an add and a store. Two threads can both
load 41, both add, and both store 42 — one increment vanishes. That is a lost
update, and with 50,000 iterations across four threads you will see thousands
of them.

`Atomics.add(view, 0, 1)` is one indivisible operation and returns the value
*before* the add.

## Hint 2

A `SharedArrayBuffer` passed in `workerData` is not cloned — both sides map
the same memory. That is the exception to everything else in this sector:

```ts
const shared = new Int32Array(new SharedArrayBuffer(4));
new Worker(src, { eval: true, workerData: { shared } });
```

Send the `Int32Array` itself; the view is rebuilt over the same backing store
on the other side.

## Hint 3

For the waiting, the simplest correct answer is the one you already have: a
promise per worker that resolves on `exit`, then `Promise.all`. Once every
thread has exited, every increment has happened, so a plain `Atomics.load` is
enough to read the result.

The decision left to you: whether to read the counter with `Atomics.load` or
plain indexing once the workers are gone. One of those is defensible for a
reason you should be able to state.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the memory model. JavaScript's is relaxed, borrowed from
C++11: a plain read is allowed to see a stale value, and the compiler is
allowed to keep it in a register across a loop. `Atomics` operations are
sequentially consistent with each other, which is why they are the only thing
you can reason about across threads.

That is the answer to "why not just use a normal variable" in one sentence.

## Hint 2

If you try the more advanced waiting strategy, know the trap. `Atomics.wait`
throws `TypeError: Atomics.wait cannot be called in this context` on the main
thread — deliberately, because blocking the loop is the disease. The async
form exists:

```ts
const r = Atomics.waitAsync(view, 0, expected);
// r.async === false and r.value === "not-equal" when it already changed
```

Handling only `r.async === true` gives you a wait that hangs whenever the
workers were fast enough to finish first — a race you will lose one run in a
hundred.

## Hint 3

For the counting itself, note that a worker doing 50,000 atomic adds is a
genuinely different cost profile from 50,000 plain adds — atomics are a
locked instruction and defeat some optimisations. In real code you would keep
a thread-local total and do one `Atomics.add` at the end. Here the point is
correctness, but the optimisation is worth knowing and worth a comment.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A pool is three lists and one rule. The lists: idle workers, busy workers, a
queue of waiting tasks. The rule: after anything finishes, look at the queue
and the idle list and start whatever you can.

Write that "pump" function first, call it from every state change, and the
rest is bookkeeping.

## Hint 2

A queued task is a promise you have not settled yet, so you must store its
`resolve` and `reject` alongside its payload:

```ts
type Pending = { payload: unknown; resolve: (v: never) => void; reject: (e: unknown) => void };
```

`Promise.withResolvers()` (Node 22) gives you the three pieces without the
executor dance.

## Hint 3

For each dispatch, attach `once("message")` and `once("error")` handlers,
settle the pending task, then move the worker from busy back to idle and pump
again. Do the move in a `finally`-like path that runs on both outcomes.

The decision left to you: when a worker *errors*, is it still safe to reuse?
The generous answer keeps the pool full; the strict answer replaces the
worker. Pick one and say why in a comment.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter from the failure the exercise exists to prevent. Pool of 2, two tasks
that reject, no release on the error path: both workers stay marked busy
forever. Every later `run` queues and never starts, and the symptom is a
service that goes quiet rather than one that errors — no exception, no log,
just requests that stop being answered.

## Hint 2

The second failure is subtler: releasing a worker *twice*. If you release on
`message` and again on `exit`, the same worker lands in the idle list twice
and two tasks get dispatched to it at once. Their replies then arrive on one
port and the pool matches them to the wrong promises.

A per-dispatch settle-once guard is the same tool as ex1, in a different
costume.

## Hint 3

`close()` has a real design question inside it. Queued-but-not-started tasks:
do they run, or do they reject? Both are legitimate — draining is friendlier,
rejecting is faster to shut down — but a `close()` that terminates workers
while tasks are in flight and leaves those promises pending forever is not.
Whatever you choose, every promise the pool handed out must settle.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 7 — cancelling work that will not yield

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function runCancellable(
  iterations: number,
  signal: AbortSignal,
  options?: { graceMs?: number },
): Promise<{ status: "completed" | "cancelled" | "terminated"; done: number }>
```

Start a worker that loops `iterations` times, checking a shared `Int32Array`
flag every 1024 iterations. When `signal` aborts:

- set the flag; if the worker notices, it posts `{ cancelled: true, done }`
  and you resolve with `status: "cancelled"`;
- if it has not exited within `graceMs` (default 50), call `terminate()` and
  resolve with `status: "terminated"` and the last `done` you were told about
  (0 if none).

If the loop finishes first, resolve with `status: "completed"` and
`done === iterations`. An already-aborted signal resolves as `"cancelled"`
with `done: 0` and starts no worker. Remove the abort listener on every path.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc01_worker_threads ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

There are two different things called cancellation here and you need both.
The cooperative one is a flag the worker chooses to read. The forcible one is
`terminate()`, which stops the thread at V8's next interrupt point and cannot
be relied on to be prompt — or, for a genuinely tight loop, to happen at all.

The grace period is the seam between them.

## Hint 2

The flag lives in shared memory because it is the only thing both threads can
see:

```ts
const flag = new Int32Array(new SharedArrayBuffer(4));
signal.addEventListener("abort", () => Atomics.store(flag, 0, 1), { once: true });
```

Inside the worker, `(i & 1023) === 0 && Atomics.load(flag, 0) === 1` is the
check. The mask is a cheap "every 1024th iteration" without a modulo.

## Hint 3

The grace timer starts when the abort arrives, not when the worker starts, and
it must be cleared when the worker settles first — otherwise your process
holds a timer for `graceMs` after every completed job, and in a test suite
that is the thing that keeps the runner alive at the end.

The decision left to you: what `done` should say after a forced terminate. The
worker cannot tell you anything once it is dead, so you either track progress
messages as they arrive or admit you do not know.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from why `terminate()` alone is not the answer, because that is the
interview question hiding in this exercise. V8 terminates execution at
interrupt checks. A loop that allocates or calls out hits them constantly; an
optimised numeric loop may not hit one for a long time, and `while (true);`
may never hit one. So `terminate()` is a request with no deadline, and any
timeout built purely on it can hang.

## Hint 2

Now consider the opposite failure: a cooperative-only design. If the worker
is code you do not control — a plugin, a user-supplied transform, a library
that ignores your flag — nothing will ever check it, and your cancellation is
a suggestion. That is why real runners escalate, and why the status enum in
this exercise has three values rather than two.

## Hint 3

Sequence the settlement carefully. The worker may post `{ cancelled: true }`
at the same moment your grace timer fires; both paths must go through one
settle-once guard, and the first one wins. Test it by setting `graceMs` to 0
and to 10_000 and checking the result is coherent in both cases.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 8 — progress on a channel of its own

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function runWithProgress(
  steps: number,
  onProgress: (completed: number) => void,
): Promise<{ steps: number; updates: number }>
```

Create a `MessageChannel`, transfer `port2` into the worker, and have the
worker report each completed step on that port while sending only the final
result on the main port. `updates` is how many progress messages you received;
`onProgress` is called with each completed count, in order (1, 2, 3, ...).

The progress port must be closed when the job settles, and no progress
callback may fire after the promise resolves.

```ts
const seen: number[] = [];
await runWithProgress(3, (n) => seen.push(n));
// resolves { steps: 3, updates: 3 }; seen === [1, 2, 3]
```

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc01_worker_threads ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`new MessageChannel()` gives you two connected ports. Keep `port1`, transfer
`port2` to the worker, and the worker posts to the port it was given. A
`MessagePort` is transferable, so it goes in the transfer list exactly like an
`ArrayBuffer`.

You can pass it through `workerData` as well — `workerData` supports transfer
via the `transferList` option on the constructor.

## Hint 2

A received port is inert until you start reading it:

```ts
channel.port1.on("message", (n) => onProgress(n));   // implies start()
```

Attaching a `message` listener starts the port; using `port.onmessage =` also
starts it, and `receiveMessageOnPort` does not. A port nobody starts buffers
messages and keeps the loop alive.

## Hint 3

Closing matters twice: `port1.close()` when you settle, so no late progress
message reaches the caller after their promise resolved, and the worker's own
port closing when it exits. An open port is a referenced handle, and a
referenced handle stops `node` from exiting.

The decision left to you: whether to count updates in the handler or ask the
worker to number them. One of those survives a dropped message.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask why a second channel is worth the trouble at all, because you could tag
messages on the main port with `{ type: "progress" }`.

Two answers. First, separation of concerns: the thing that consumes progress
can be handed `port1` and know nothing about workers, pools or your result
protocol. Second, lifetime: closing the progress port ends updates without
touching the job, which is exactly what you want when a client disconnects but
the work is still worth finishing.

## Hint 2

The failure to design against is the late callback. The worker posts step 3,
posts the result, and exits. Your promise resolves on the result — but the
progress message may still be sitting in the port's queue, and it will be
delivered on a later turn of the loop, calling the caller's function after
they believed the job was done.

Closing `port1` in the same synchronous block as the resolve is what prevents
it.

## Hint 3

Ordering is a property of the channel, not of your code: messages on one port
are delivered in the order they were posted. So `onProgress` sees 1, 2, 3
without any sequencing work — as long as every update goes down the same port.
Split progress across two ports and that guarantee is gone.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Build it in the order the data flows: the worker protocol first (one message
in with the buffer and a flag, one message out with the buffer and a count),
then the pool around it, then the abort handling on top.

Trying to hold all three in your head at once is what makes this feel hard.

## Hint 2

Each job needs its own flag, but the worker is reused — so the flag cannot
live in `workerData`. Send it with the job:

```ts
worker.postMessage({ buffer, flag }, [buffer]);
```

A `SharedArrayBuffer` in a `postMessage` is shared, not copied, and it does
not go in the transfer list. Mixing the two up is the error you will hit
first.

## Hint 3

Aborting a queued job is a queue operation, not a worker operation: find the
entry, remove it, reject it. Aborting a running job is a memory write:
`Atomics.store(flag, 0, 1)`. The same `AbortSignal` handler therefore has to
know which state the job is in — keep that state on the job record and branch
on it.

The decision left to you: after a cancelled job, is the worker reusable? Its
loop returned normally, so it is — but say why in a comment, because the
opposite argument (unknown state) is what you would make if it had thrown.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter from the state machine. A job is in exactly one of: `queued`, `running`,
`settled`. Every event — dispatch, reply, abort, close — is a transition, and
every transition must be legal from exactly the states you allow.

Write the table before the code. Most bugs in this challenge are transitions
you did not think about, such as an abort arriving after the reply.

## Hint 2

The transfer makes the abort path subtle. When a job is cancelled mid-run, the
worker still owns the buffer, and it must transfer it back for the caller to
see the partial work. So "cancelled" cannot mean "stop listening" — you still
await one final message. A design that rejects immediately on abort loses the
bytes and, worse, leaves a worker permanently marked busy.

## Hint 3

`close()` has three groups to handle and they are handled differently: queued
jobs reject now, running jobs are awaited (they will settle on their own),
idle workers terminate. If you find yourself wanting to terminate a busy
worker, notice that its promise would then never settle — the same bug as
ex6's `close`, dressed up.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

This is ex1 with the abstraction removed. There, four events collapsed into
resolve-or-reject; here they stay four, and the promise always resolves.

Notice what that changes: an observer that rejects on `error` would force
every caller into a `try`/`catch` to ask a question that has no failure mode.

## Hint 2

The listener set is the same, and identity still matters:

```ts
const onExit = (code: number) => settle({ kind: "exit", code });
worker.on("exit", onExit);
// ... later
worker.off("exit", onExit);
```

An inline arrow in `off` removes nothing, which you can see for yourself with
`worker.listenerCount("exit")` before and after.

## Hint 3

One settle-once guard, four handlers, cleanup inside the guard. The ordering
guarantee you are relying on — `error` is emitted before `exit` — is what
makes "first event wins" the right rule rather than an arbitrary one.

The decision left to you: what to do if the worker has *already* exited when
`settleWorker` is called. There is no replay, so decide whether to detect it
(`worker.threadId` is `-1` after exit) or to document the precondition.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from where you would use this. A supervisor that restarts workers needs
to know *why* one went away, because the response differs: an `error` is a bug
to log with a stack; an `exit` with code 0 is a worker that finished; an
`exit` with a non-zero code you did not ask for is a crash to count towards a
backoff.

Collapsing all of that into "the promise rejected" throws away the input to
that decision.

## Hint 2

`messageerror` is the one people have never seen. It fires when a message
arrives that cannot be deserialised in this isolate — most realistically a
`SharedArrayBuffer` sent to a context that forbids it, or a value from a
version mismatch. It is rare, it is not an `error`, and a worker can keep
running afterwards.

That is exactly why it deserves its own tag rather than being folded into the
error case.

## Hint 3

Test the ordering claim rather than trusting it. Attach counters for all four
events on a worker that throws and log what arrives: you will see `error`,
then `exit` with 1. Then do the same with `process.exit(0)` inside the worker
and watch `exit` arrive alone. Those two runs are the whole specification.

# V3·NC2 — Child processes, spawning and stdio

The previous sector moved expensive JavaScript onto another thread. This one
moves work out of your process entirely: `ffmpeg`, `git`, `pdftotext`, a
Python script, another Node program, `psql`. The mechanism is older than Node
and older than JavaScript — `fork`, `exec`, three file descriptors and a wait
status — and Node's API is a thin, occasionally leaky wrapper over it.

The leaks are where the bugs live. A pipe that nobody reads fills up and the
child blocks forever. A shell that nobody asked for turns a filename into a
command. An exit code of `null` means something completely different from an
exit code of `0`. None of that is exotic; all of it appears the first week a
service shells out to anything.

## Concept — four functions, one of which you should usually use

```ts
import { spawn, exec, execFile, fork } from "node:child_process";
```

**`spawn(file, args, options)`** is the primitive. It starts a program, gives
you streams, and never involves a shell unless you ask. Output arrives as it
is produced, so memory is bounded by whatever you do with it. This is the
default answer.

**`exec(command, options)`** takes a *command string*, runs it through
`/bin/sh` (or `cmd.exe`), buffers all of stdout and stderr in memory, and
calls back at the end. Two consequences, both bad if you did not want them:
the string is interpreted by a shell, and the output has a 1 MiB default
`maxBuffer` after which the child is killed and you get
`ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER`. Convenient for a one-liner in a build
script; wrong for a service.

**`execFile(file, args, options)`** is `exec` without the shell: buffering and
a callback, but arguments stay arguments. If you want the convenience and not
the injection surface, this is the one.

**`fork(modulePath)`** is `spawn` of a *Node* module with an IPC channel
already wired: `child.send(value)` on one side, `process.on("message")` on the
other. Values are serialised as JSON by default, which quietly turns `Date`
into a string and drops `undefined`; `serialization: "advanced"` switches to
the same structured-clone serialiser worker threads use.

```ts
const child = spawn(process.execPath, ["-e", "console.log(process.argv[1])", "hello"]);
child.stdout.setEncoding("utf8");
for await (const chunk of child.stdout) process.stdout.write(chunk);
```

## Concept — the stdio triple

Every child gets an array of descriptors, and `options.stdio` describes them:

- `"pipe"` (the default) — Node creates a pipe and gives you
  `child.stdin` / `child.stdout` / `child.stderr` as streams;
- `"inherit"` — the child writes straight to your own descriptors, so its
  output appears in your terminal and you get no stream;
- `"ignore"` — `/dev/null`;
- `"ipc"` — the message channel `fork` sets up, available to `spawn` as
  `stdio: ["pipe", "pipe", "pipe", "ipc"]`;
- a `Stream` or an fd number — plumb the child straight into a file or socket.

The trap in that list is `"pipe"` with nobody reading. A pipe holds 64 KB on
Linux; when it is full, the child's next `write` blocks. If you are waiting
for the child to exit while the child is waiting for you to read, that is a
deadlock, and it is *the* classic child-process bug. Either consume the
streams, or use `"ignore"`, or use `"inherit"`.

## Concept — how a child ends

```ts
child.on("exit", (code, signal) => { /* code | signal, never both */ });
child.on("close", (code, signal) => { /* stdio is finished too */ });
child.on("error", (error) => { /* it never started, or kill() failed */ });
```

`code` is a number when the program returned normally, and `null` when it was
killed — in which case `signal` is the string (`"SIGTERM"`, `"SIGKILL"`). Code
`0` is success; anything else is the program's own idea of failure. And
`error` is not "the program failed": it is "there was no program", the classic
being `ENOENT` when the binary is not on `PATH`.

`exit` fires when the process is gone; `close` fires when its stdio streams
have also ended. Those are usually microseconds apart and occasionally are
not — if you collect stdout and read it in `exit`, you can miss the last
chunk. Collect in `close`.

## Concept — the shell is a decision, not a detail

```ts
spawn("grep", [userInput, "notes.txt"]);                    // safe
spawn(`grep ${userInput} notes.txt`, { shell: true });      // remote code execution
```

With an argument array the kernel receives your arguments verbatim: a value of
`; rm -rf /` is a search string, not a command. With `shell: true` the string
is parsed by `sh`, and everything the shell finds meaningful — `;`, `&&`, `|`,
backticks, `$(...)`, globs — is meaningful.

Windows complicates this honestly rather than theoretically. There is no
`execve`; the OS takes a command *line* and the program parses it, so Node has
to quote for you, and `.cmd`/`.bat` files can only be run through `cmd.exe`.
Node 18.20.2/20.12.2/21.7.3 shipped a fix for CVE-2024-27980, where crafted
arguments could escape that quoting on Windows; the current behaviour is to
require `shell: true` for batch files and quote more aggressively. The rule
that survives all of it: **arguments in an array, `shell` only when you mean
it, and never interpolate user input into a command string.**

## Exercise 1 — run a program, capture everything

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `runCommand(file, args)` spawns without a shell and
resolves with `{ code, signal, stdout, stderr }` collected to completion.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc02_child_processes ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — lines, not chunks

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `createLineSplitter(onLine)` turns arbitrary chunk
boundaries into whole lines, holds the partial tail, and flushes it at the
end.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc02_child_processes ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — a timeout that escalates

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `runWithTimeout(file, args, ms)` sends `SIGTERM` at
the deadline, `SIGKILL` after a grace period, and reports which one ended it.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc02_child_processes ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — building an argv you can defend

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `planSpawn(command)` decides whether a shell is
required, rejects interpolation attempts, and returns a `{ file, args, shell }`
spec.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc02_child_processes ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — request and response over IPC

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `createRpcChild()` spawns a Node child with an `ipc`
descriptor and correlates replies to requests by id.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc02_child_processes ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — many commands, bounded

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `runAll(specs, { concurrency })` runs at most N
children at once and returns results in input order.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc02_child_processes ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — what actually happened

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `classifyOutcome(outcome)` maps an exit code, a signal
or a spawn error onto `"ok"`, `"nonzero"`, `"signal"` or `"spawn-failed"`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc02_child_processes ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — writing to a child that stops listening

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `pipeThrough(file, args, input)` writes to the child's
stdin, survives `EPIPE`, and still returns whatever the child produced.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc02_child_processes ex8
```

## Challenge — a small job runner

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. `createRunner({ concurrency, timeoutMs })`
combines the queue, the escalating timeout and line-by-line streaming into one
API.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc02_child_processes challenge
```

## Review — exec's semantics, by hand

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. `execCapture(file, args, { maxBuffer })`
reproduces `exec`'s truncation rule: kill the child and reject once the output
exceeds the limit.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc02_child_processes review1
```

# Reading - node/v3nc02_child_processes

Child processes are the oldest concurrency primitive there is, and Node's API
is close enough to the kernel that the kernel's rules still apply to you.

## Notes

**`spawn` does not use a shell and that is the feature.** Every convenience
function above it — `exec`, and `spawn` with `shell: true` — buys ergonomics
with an interpreter that treats your data as code. The moment any part of the
command comes from a request, a filename, a branch name or an environment
variable, the array form is the only defensible choice.

**Buffering is a memory decision.** `exec` holds all output in memory and caps
it at `maxBuffer` (1 MiB since Node 12). Hit the cap and the child is killed
with `SIGTERM` and the callback gets an error whose `code` is
`ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER` — with the partial output still attached,
which people forget. A command producing a 500 MB tarball on stdout must be
streamed; there is no `maxBuffer` large enough to make that a good idea.

**`exit` versus `close`.** `exit` means the process is gone. `close` means its
stdio streams have ended as well. Read your collected output in `close` and
the last chunk is always there; read it in `exit` and it usually is.

**`code === null` is not `code === 0`.** A killed process has no exit code, and
`signal` tells you which one ended it. Code written as `if (code !== 0)` treats
a `SIGKILL` as success, because `null !== 0` is true but the branch people
write is `if (!code)`.

**Signals are POSIX and Windows is not.** `child.kill("SIGTERM")` on Windows
terminates the process immediately — there is no graceful handler, because
there are no signals. `SIGKILL` and `SIGTERM` both map onto `TerminateProcess`.
Any design that relies on a child cleaning up after `SIGTERM` needs a
different mechanism (a message over IPC, a sentinel file) to work on Windows.

**Killing a process does not kill its children.** `child.kill()` signals one
pid. A shell that spawned a program leaves that program running as an orphan.
`detached: true` puts the child in its own process group, and then
`process.kill(-child.pid, "SIGTERM")` signals the whole group — the reliable
way to stop a tree.

**`unref` and `detached` are about lifetimes.** `child.unref()` stops the child
keeping the parent's event loop alive; `detached: true` plus `unref()` plus
`stdio: "ignore"` is how you launch something that outlives you.

## ex1 — the honest wrapper

Collecting to completion is four events and one rule: resolve in `close`, not
`exit`. Concatenating strings per chunk is the other half — `Buffer.concat` of
an array of chunks handles multi-byte characters split across a boundary,
which `chunk.toString()` per chunk does not.

## ex2 — chunk boundaries are arbitrary

A pipe delivers whatever it has. `"hello\nwor"` and `"ld\n"` is a perfectly
legal way to receive two lines, and every naive `split("\n")` loses `world`.
Keeping the tail is the fix; flushing it at the end is the part people forget,
which is why the last line of output goes missing exactly when it has no
trailing newline.

## ex3 — polite, then not

`SIGTERM` asks; `SIGKILL` tells. A timeout that only sends `SIGTERM` can hang
forever on a program that ignores it, and a timeout that goes straight to
`SIGKILL` prevents any cleanup the child might legitimately do. The two-stage
pattern with a small grace period is what every process supervisor implements,
including Docker (10 seconds) and Kubernetes (`terminationGracePeriodSeconds`,
30 by default).

## ex4 — the injection surface, written down

The exercise is a policy, not a parser: decide when a shell is genuinely
needed, refuse the cases where a string is being built from parts, and be
explicit about the Windows batch-file exception. Writing the policy as code is
the point — "we are careful" is not a control.

## ex5 — IPC and correlation

A message channel is unordered with respect to *requests*: two outstanding
calls come back in whatever order the child finishes them. Correlation ids are
the standard answer, and the `Map` from id to resolver is the standard shape.
The detail worth keeping: JSON serialisation means `undefined` disappears and
`Date` arrives as a string, so a protocol that survives is one you defined
rather than one you assumed.

## ex6 — concurrency without a library

The pattern from `d07_concurrency_control`, now spawning processes: N workers
pulling from a shared index, results written to their own slot so order is
positional. Bounding it matters more here than for promises — each child is
megabytes of RSS and a scheduler entry, and an unbounded fan-out over 5,000
files is a fork bomb you wrote yourself.

## ex7 — the four endings

Making the taxonomy explicit forces the distinctions the API blurs: a spawn
error is not a failure of the program, a signal is not an exit code, and a
non-zero code is the program telling you something rather than the platform.
Supervisors branch on exactly this.

## ex8 — EPIPE is normal

Write into a child that has exited and you get `EPIPE` on the stream. It is
not a bug in your code, it is the pipe telling you the reader is gone — `head`
does it to everything. The correct behaviour is to stop writing and keep the
output you already have, not to fail the whole call.

## challenge — the three together

Queue, deadline, streaming. The interesting interaction is that a timeout must
kill a child whose output you are mid-stream, and the line splitter must still
flush what it has: a timed-out job that reports nothing is much less useful
than one that reports the 40 lines it managed.

## review1 — implementing exec's rule

Reproducing `maxBuffer` teaches what the convenience cost. You count bytes as
they arrive, kill at the threshold, and still return the truncated output — and
by the end you can say precisely why `exec` is fine for `git rev-parse` and
wrong for `docker logs`.

## Further reading

- [`child_process` — Node.js API docs](https://nodejs.org/api/child_process.html) — every option, including `stdio`, `detached` and `serialization`.
- [`Signals` — Node.js process docs](https://nodejs.org/api/process.html#signal-events) — what you can catch, and the Windows caveats.
- [Node.js security release, April 2024](https://nodejs.org/en/blog/vulnerability/april-2024-security-releases) — CVE-2024-27980 and Windows argument escaping.
- [`Stream` — Node.js API docs](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html) — the pipe semantics behind child stdio.
- [POSIX `wait` status](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/wait.2.html) — where exit code versus signal comes from.
